item.title: Evidence-Based Ways to Add Gratitude to Your Thanksgiving
item.description:
Gratitude

Evidence-Based Ways to Add Gratitude to Your Thanksgiving

Studies identify specific steps to inject gratitude and improve your life.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Research clearly establishes that gratitude promotes well-being.
  • Research also demonstrates that it's possible to encourage gratitude in people of all ages and backgrounds.
  • It's been proven that an attitude of gratitude leads to prosocial behaviors.
Source: lilit/Adobe Stock

More than 90% of Americans celebrate Thanksgiving – typically with roasted turkeys, football games, and family gatherings. It’s widely considered the biggest and busiest holiday for travel, and it’s commonly viewed as the start of the holiday shopping season. Beyond all of these traditions, research shows there are major benefits to remembering the sentiment that accompanies Thanksgiving: gratitude.

The research clearly establishes that gratitude promotes well-being. While we may feel thankful for something specific, like a gift or a meal, a broader outlook of gratitude — the mindset of noticing and appreciating the positives in your life — is proven to protect people from psychological distress.

“Gratitude has been shown to have many benefits: Grateful people are happier, less envious, sleep better, are more resilient when facing trauma, and need fewer visits to the doctor,” explained Cornell social psychologist Tom Gilovich, director of the Judgment and Belief Lab. “The benefits of gratitude, furthermore, extend to those who cross paths with grateful Individuals, as grateful individuals are more generous to others.”

The evidence on the benefits of gratitude continues to build. A 2023 systematic review combined the data from 44 articles that included more than 16,500 participants to look for connections between gratitude and life satisfaction. It found a strong connection between dispositional gratitude — a general tendency to notice, appreciate, and respond with grateful emotions in your daily life — and life satisfaction. It also found that gratitude at earlier points in life predicted life satisfaction later in life.

There’s a growing body of research demonstrating that it's possible to encourage gratitude in people of all ages and backgrounds. Another systematic review from 2023 combined 64 randomized-controlled studies measuring interventions designed to boost feelings of gratitude in participants. It found that, on the whole, the interventions led to more feeling of gratitude, fewer symptoms of anxiety and depression, greater life satisfaction, and more positive and lower psychological pain scores.

Despite the research, critics question whether gratitude could also make people complacent. The concern stems from the idea that gratitude can create feelings of contentment, which may lead to a lack of action.

A recent study published by Cornell researchers including Gilovich took on this argument. Researchers analyzed three separate data sets: a survey of more than 2,000 Americans, a longitudinal study of more than 200,000 people from 22 countries, and a field study that surveyed individuals at blood drives and flu shot clinics. They found that people who felt grateful were more likely to engage in costly prosocial actions.

“Although some have expressed a concern that feeling grateful might make people feel satisfied and therefore complacent about pressing societal problems, research shows that that concern is misplaced,” Gilovich said. “Grateful people are more likely to volunteer their time at civic and religious organizations, donate money to charity, and participate in blood drives. Gratitude not only makes you feel good, but it helps you live up to your best self and be a better member of society."

Gratitude in action

The research is clear: Gratitude provides a wide array of benefits, so consider focusing on gratitude this Thanksgiving. Here are some ways:

  • If your family goes around the table to say what they’re grateful for, encourage guests to be specific. Research shows that naming a circumstance or act of kindness that you are grateful for is more likely to generate the positive outcomes associated with gratitude.
  • Behavioral expressions of gratitude like helping in the kitchen or shoveling someone’s walkway boost psychological well-being and social connection more than words alone. Consider finding a way for your family to put their gratitude into action on Thanksgiving by volunteering at a soup kitchen or visiting an elderly neighbor.
  • Studies in positive psychology find that writing a specific letter detailing how someone impacted your life and sharing it with them produces significant spikes in happiness and reduces in depressive symptoms. Consider asking family members to write and share letters of gratitude in honor of Thanksgiving.

The take-home message: There is no doubt that gratitude is good for you. As Thanksgiving approaches, consider how you could put gratitude into action in your household.

item.title: What Poison Ivy Teaches Us About Environmental Grief
item.description:
Grief

What Poison Ivy Teaches Us About Environmental Grief

Grief for a wounded planet needs heroes, not villains.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Environmental and political grief are natural responses to ecological and social breakdown.
  • Grief that isn’t psychologically tended to can push us into survival states and extremism.
  • Like the Justice League, we heal and act best together, from awareness rather than fear.
Source: Photo by Oleksii S on Unsplash

Poison Ivy may be the only Batman villain whose cause many readers quietly agree with.

In her origin story from Batman comics, Dr. Pamela Isley (Poison Ivy) was once a passionate scientist. However, she was injected with toxins that merged her with plant life. She can control vegetation and feel the pain of plants directly.1 Driven by empathic distress, she fights environmental abuse and political negligence. Archetypally, she embodies both the grief and the fury of a wounded Earth.

Her grief reflects emotions many of us share; the research literature captures how people commonly feel sadness, fear, anger, helplessness, and profound grief in response to ecological loss.2 This is closely tied to the experience of solastalgia, or the anguish of watching a cherished home environment deteriorate until it no longer offers the solace it once did.

The grief of a wounded Earth

Environmental grief and climate-related trauma are natural and instinctive responses to climate breakdown.3 They arise from tangible losses of ecosystems, wildlife, homes, jobs, and communities. They also arise from losses that are harder to see, such as diminished trust, a loss of faith in the future, and a deeper psycho-spiritual disconnection from Earth itself.

Poison Ivy is also a figure of political grief. She is driven by moral outrage at governance that permits deforestation, pollution, and the exploitation of the natural world. Environmental grief often intersects with political grief, especially as climate change and environmental breakdown places a far greater burden on disadvantaged communities and developing countries.4 Subsequently, growing numbers of people are questioning values that give personhood to corporations but not to the natural world.

Poison Ivy accurately shows how these losses can be felt on an intensely personal level, one that penetrates us to the core of our being.

Why extremism is poisonous

Grief, hopelessness, and despair can push us into survival states marked by defensiveness, psychological inflexibility, and absolutist thinking.5 Over time, these experiences can lead people toward extremist positions, social alienation, and political polarization.6 Poison Ivy’s impulsive, destructive choices do not create meaningful collective change. Her over-identification with plants causes her to lose touch with her own humanity.

In troubling times, it can be tempting to imagine that we need a figure like Poison Ivy. This supervillain fantasy will not solve the ecological crisis, though, or meaningfully comfort our grieving hearts.

The world has already experienced enough destructive authoritarianism that violates all traditional cultural wisdom. Violence will only make problems worse, and coercion entrenches polarization and resistance.6 Tragically, supervillains embody the same cycles of harm they claim to oppose. Without an ethical framework, supervillains impose rigid ideologies that oppose cooperation, respect, dignity, and mutual understanding.

Source: Photo by Markus Spiske on Unsplash

The call for a Justice League

The environmental crisis and the ongoing tear in our political systems evoke a great deal of fear, which is exactly why we need superheroes. The Justice League from DC Comics is a diverse group of superheroes who unite against threats too large for any one of them to handle. Despite differing ideologies, they preserve a sense of common humanity.

Adopting a stance of common humanity does not require compromising deeply held values or excusing abuses of power.6 Instead, it means focusing on our intention to connect rather than our need to defend. Many Indigenous worldviews express this through four guiding values: relationship, responsibility, reciprocity, and redistribution.7

Over 40 years ago, Roger Walsh urged us to face collective existential threats from a place of psychological self-awareness rather than fear or shadow.8 External change is most effective when it is fuelled by inner transformation and by tending to our own unresolved losses. Furthermore, crises benefit from level-headed individuals who are respectful, strive to minimize harm, utilize ethical frameworks, and maintain unwavering integrity. In other words, people who can embody and psychologically integrate the qualities of a superhero are what the world needs.

When we can metabolize our widespread environmental and political grief, we create inner space and presence. That space awakens us to life, love, and interdependence, and to the ability to re-imagine the future. No one is also meant to face this grief alone. Our collective moment of reckoning has arrived, and we need all the superheroes we can muster.

This piece draws on my book chapter, “From Poison Ivy to the Justice League: A Psychological Approach to Environmental and Political Grief,” in Superhero Grief and the Multiverse of Loss: Considerations and Case Studies, edited by Jill Harrington and Darcy Harris (Routledge, 2026). This new collection uses superheroes and the multiverse to explore how non-death loss impacts our psychology.9

item.title: How to Not Lose Your Cool This Holiday Season
item.description:
Anger

How to Not Lose Your Cool This Holiday Season

Try these anger management techniques to stay even-keeled through the New Year.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic anger can impair cardiovascular health, immune functioning, and cause interpersonal challenges.
  • Anger management strategies can help prevent it from harming yourself and others.
  • Distraction, mindfulness, visualization, and cold temperature exposure can help manage anger.

While the holidays can bring a great deal of joy, they can also trigger anger in a lot of people. Think: having to face difficult people during annual social gatherings, being stuck in traffic or stranded at an airport because of delays, or feeling underappreciated for all the effort you’ve put into a holiday that others may not have acknowledged.

Anger is a powerful emotion. Chronically angry people are more likely to suffer from heart disease, diabetes, and impaired immune functioning. They're also more likely to have unhappy marriages, be lonelier, and struggle at work.

Anger itself is not the problem. It's a normal and healthy emotion like any other. But when it goes unchecked, it can make us do and say things that cause irreparable damage or act in ways we deeply regret.

To help you keep your cool this holiday season, here are five anger management techniques you can start using—today.

1. Name Five Things That Are Blue

Look around your surrounding environment and try to find five things that are blue. Alternatively, you can seek out five things that begin with the letter A. Either approach helps shift your attention from the source of anger to a neutral stimulus. This brief break helps you de-escalate through cognitive shifting by allowing your emotions to cool down. The more time we spend ruminating and focusing on what’s upsetting us, the more hotheaded we can become. Distraction techniques like these interrupt that anger-rumination-explosion cycle, reducing activity in the amygdala and allowing our heart rates and blood pressure to come back to baseline.

2. Boxed Breathing

Inhale all the way. Hold your breath for three to four seconds. Exhale all the way (try to make your exhale longer than your inhale). Hold your breath again at the bottom of that exhale for another three to four seconds. Repeat several times until you feel a reduction in distress. This breathwork technique and others like it help regulate the nervous system by increasing activity within the parasympathetic nervous system—the branch of the autonomic nervous system undergirding resting and digesting functions—and downshifting activity within the sympathetic (fight/flight) nervous system.

3. Physicalization

When you feel yourself getting heated, try to imagine the anger you’re feeling as an object in your body. First, where is it? Then, what does it look like? Feel like? What’s its temperature and texture; its weight? Be as descriptive as you can. Then, take a deep breath in and, with that breath, imagine creating space around the object in your body. On the exhale, imagine breathing out its intensity—almost like you’re cooling off the object of anger in your body.

Many studies have found that mindfulness techniques such as this help to ease anger, in part by creating some distance between you and the anger itself, so that anger doesn’t take you on as great a roller coaster ride. Taking time to visualize and work with the emotion in the body also helps slow you down, so you don’t knee-jerked-ly blurt out something nasty or otherwise act impulsively in a way that may haunt you (and possibly ruin Thanksgiving dinner).

4. Tip Your Temperature

If you feel yourself starting to get worked up—you're gritting your teeth, your face is flushed, your breathing is shallow, your fists are clenched—see if you can excuse yourself to splash some very cold water on your face or hold some ice cubes to your chest or your temples. If you’re in a part of the world where it’s cold during the holiday season, go take a walk outside in the icy air. Exposure to very cold temperatures helps to trigger the diving reflex, which quickly lowers heart rate and can essentially shock your body back into a less elevated state.

5. Force Field Visualization

This one is especially helpful for dealing with difficult people over the holidays. If you’re surrounded by folks who aren’t aligned with you politically, can be quite rude, or make unnecessary comments about your life, body, or any other personal aspect, imagine a force field around you. Really go deep with the visualization here. What color is the force field? What is it made of—ice? Fire? Laser beams? Does it make a noise? Then, imagine the difficult person’s (or persons’) statements bouncing off of the force field (better yet, if they make a funny noise when they do so), leaving you safe and protected. You can go the extra mile and imagine the statements bouncing back and tripping the other person, spilling all over them, or whatever other amusing visual will bring you more of a smile than a grimace.

If You're Still Really Struggling...

All of these techniques can be useful in moments of high frustration leading to intense anger. (I use them with my clients, and also with myself.) If you find yourself becoming angry quite often or if you find it particularly challenging to de-escalate and not do things you later feel badly about, it may be worth connecting with a therapist who can help you practice skills like these as well as do some deeper work around the origins of any chronic anger you may be struggling with. Don’t hesitate to get help if this is the case. Your heart health will thank you if you do.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Weight Gain During Long-Term Antipsychotic Use
item.description:
Psychosis

Weight Gain During Long-Term Antipsychotic Use

Personal Perspective: The challenge of weight gain with antipsychotic use.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Weight gain from medication can intensify self-blame and stigma around mental illness.
  • Prioritizing mental health sometimes requires accepting difficult side effects like weight gain.
  • Focusing on health and fitness has greater benefits than simply chasing numbers on the scale.
Source: CineLens/peopleimages/AdobeStock

Most antipsychotics cause some degree of weight gain. They are generally classified into three categories according to the degree of weight gain each causes. Weight gain caused by antipsychotics can be a deterrent to using them, or a motivation to go off antipsychotics prematurely. For someone like me who has been on antipsychotics for 26 years, I have experienced a lifetime of managing weight fluctuation, gaining a good deal of weight and then losing it a few times. Here is an account of my journey of weight gain and loss while taking antipsychotics and what I have gleaned from these experiences.

Blaming Weight Gain on Yourself

My first antipsychotic was Zyprexa, which I first started taking in 2001. I was not informed by my psychiatrist at that time that this drug causes weight gain, and I was on a higher dose. Accordingly, I had no idea I was taking the antipsychotic notorious for causing the most weight gain, and the psychiatrist never shared with me the fact that the medicine could be a factor in my weight gain.

I was already so hard on myself for taking an antipsychotic in the first place, and the weight gain, which I blamed on myself, was another source of shame. I couldn’t understand why I was gaining weight when nothing had changed with how much I eat and how much I was exercising, so I felt like my life was out of control in multiple ways. It felt similar to having some sort of mental illness but not really understanding what I was up against or what I could do about it.

It’s so easy to be hard on yourself about weight gain, and it’s also so incredibly hard to properly attribute your medicine for causing it. Because of stigma, we are taught that mental illness should be under our control, just like society tells us that weight gain is really always under our control as well. Taking an antipsychotic can tug at your self-esteem, and weight gain just intensifies any tendency for low self-esteem and self-blame.

Weight Gain at the Worst Times

I was on Abilify and experienced almost no weight gain with it, so I was happy. However, I suddenly started having involuntary tongue movements with this drug after it had worked well for me for years, so I had no choice but to go back on Zyprexa, just a month or two before I started trying on wedding dresses after my engagement. As someone who was anorexic in college and still body dysmorphic, gaining a bunch of weight right before trying on wedding dresses, when most people try to be their thinnest, seemed so unfair. I took it as a sign that I would never be able to move on with my life.

I was thankful that my psychiatrist put me on a high dose of Metformin to help manage weight gain caused by Zyprexa. The Metformin felt to me like validation and acknowledgement that, yes, it’s not all my fault if I gain weight on this drug and that there are real, demonstrated ways that psychiatry acknowledges and helps us with this issue. Even with Metformin, I put on 15 pounds, but I successfully worked hard to lose it all before it was time for dress alterations. But it did feel like an unnecessary hurdle and annoying complication, a reminder that my illness is never over.

Beating the Weight Gain/Loss Cycle Mentality

I’ve gained and lost so many pounds through antipsychotic use. The weight creeps in until one day I’m forced to address it, then I go through an organized effort to lose it. Growing up, I was a competitive athlete who thought weighing 140 pounds was a lot, but for most of my adult life on antipsychotics, weighing 140 is no longer achievable, or if so, unsustainable.

I’m convinced the reason I gained over 60 pounds while pregnant with my child was due to being on Zyprexa at the time. However, I did lose the weight through walking, calorie reduction, and nursing. With the help of Metformin, I did not get gestational diabetes. I’m now on Quetiapine, and it is supposed to be a moderate weight gainer, but I don’t think I have much of an easier time keeping weight off with this drug than with Zyprexa. However, since Quetiapine is perfect for avoiding a terrible side effect I get with every other drug, there is no way I will ever take any other drug again. This time, when weight loss was called for at age 47, I needed to go on a GLP to lose it.

Health Is the Silver Lining for Me

One thing I can say about this 26-year journey of weight gain and dieting since I've been on antipsychotics is that I am healthier for it and make healthier choices. Because I have less control over my metabolism, I have made other critical health choices that will pay off in the long run in multiple ways. Giving up gluten is a big deal for me, especially with thyroid diseases, as well as giving up almost all soda and alcohol. I’ve also been a vegetarian for 20 years, for a number of reasons in addition to health. Some of these choices started as ways I could mitigate weight gain caused by antipsychotics, but they turned out to have benefited me in other very real ways.

Another huge shift for me is caring more about my health than fixating on the number on the scale. I’m no longer concerned with going back to 140—I’m more interested in longevity and keeping up with my 7-year-old son. Through my cycle of weight gain and loss, I’ve given up on the idea that success is a clothing size; it’s about my bloodwork all looking good, reducing inflammation, feeling energetic, and exercising regularly.

The Need for Control

One of the toughest aspects of serious mental illness is the elusiveness. You can’t visualize it; there is no blood test, and you may get re-diagnosed by different doctors. Sometimes there is no clear answer on what to do at all. You can’t control what effects antipsychotics have on you, and sometimes discerning what is under your control and what is being dictated by the antipsychotic is difficult. Weight gain caused by antipsychotics can feel the same way, leaving you feeling powerless and frustrated.

It’s hard and seems unfair that making the right and responsible choice for your mental health can have other health consequences. But staying on antipsychotics, even if they cause weight gain, has been critical for my full remission from schizophrenia for 15 years and for becoming a wife and mother. Unpredictable weight gain has also led me to make important health decisions for myself when it comes to food and drink that will benefit me for the rest of my life. I’ve also made other good health choices that I probably would not have made if I did not have a tendency to gain weight due to antipsychotics. I’ve also learned to lean on internal means of validation and self-esteem instead of superficial, external means.

item.title: When Therapy Forgets What It Means to Be Human
item.description:
Therapy

When Therapy Forgets What It Means to Be Human

Too much focus on diagnostic labels can make humans sound like machines.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Reducing mental health to diagnostic labels oversimplifies complex human experiences.
  • Working with machines means labeling parts and understanding physical mechanics. Humans are different.
  • Working with humans should mean addressing meaning and purpose, not just diagnostic labels and physiology.

These days, when you hear mental health professionals say that they want clients to understand their conditions better, they are usually referring to diagnostic labels. It is a shame how much mental health conditions have been reduced to labels.

If you want to understand why you are feeling down, the thinking goes, you need to understand depression. If you are nervous about things that are happening in your life, you need to understand anxiety. If you are having difficulties in social situations, you need to understand autism. And if your mood tends to fluctuate easily, you need to understand bipolar disorder.

What makes this even more troubling is how much these conditions are reduced not just to labels, but to labels related only to physical functioning. When it comes to mental health issues, the questions are often reduced to labels, and human beings are reduced to physiological machines.

It is almost as if people are treated as robots. Understand what is going wrong with a robot’s mechanics, and you can fix it.

But what if your psychological condition is just part of being human?

What if your depression is due to a lack of meaning or purpose in life? What if your anxiety is due to a very real fear caused by life being uncertain? What if your difficulties with people are due to the negative ways people act toward you, or uncertainty because social interactions do not come with any sort of guidebook? And what if your fluctuating mood is related to recognizing that you have a limited time on earth and are trying to find the best ways of navigating obstacles toward making that time meaningful?

For example, think about someone who comes to counseling feeling depressed because they spent years working toward goals that no longer seem meaningful. They may be having difficulty sleeping, have little motivation, and feel sad much of the time. Those symptoms might justify a depression diagnosis, but does that diagnosis really explain what the person is experiencing?

Understanding the person's struggle with meaning and purpose may be much more important than simply saying they have depression and need to understand that diagnosis better. Saying “you’re searching for more meaning and purpose in your life” fits more with what it means to be human than saying “you have depression.”

It is unfortunate that authors, artists, and philosophers recognize that being human involves functioning on multiple deep levels, but psychologists and counselors often do not.

Life is difficult. Life is complex. Navigating that complexity can be difficult, troubling, and emotionally taxing. Feeling like something is missing, something is lost, something is difficult to navigate, or something is meaningless can be a very real source of emotional distress.

Yet mental health professionals may not recognize this.

Medical thinking and pharmaceutical companies seem to dominate mental healthcare to a large degree, and this can lead to minimizing or abandoning altogether the idea that human beings can experience true emotional distress because they are looking for their lives to have direction, meaning, and purpose and just cannot find it.

None of this means that physiology, neurology, or medication should be ignored. It means that understanding these things is not the same as understanding a human being.

If you are seeking a therapist or counselor, this is something to keep in mind. Does the therapist or counselor reduce your suffering to just physiology or something wrong with your body or neurology? Do they seem to act primarily as a cheerleader for pharmaceutical companies, where the answer keeps coming back to medication? Or do they truly look at the complexities of what you are facing in your life?

If there is a lot of focus in your therapy or counseling on physiology and medication, this does not mean that your counselor or therapist is doing something wrong. But it may be worth bringing up. Asking your therapist or counselor whether there is room to discuss deeper questions in life can be an important step for moving therapy in a more helpful direction. It is important to consider whether you are truly being treated as a human being and not just a machine.

If we compare ourselves to machines, we know that human beings function on a much more complex level. Machines do not worry about meaning or purpose in their lives. Machines may recognize that they have an expiration date, but they do not worry about getting certain things done within that timeframe. Machines understand the tasks ahead of them and work on those tasks until the time they shut down, but they do not worry about what it means if they do not get those tasks done.

Human beings worry about living purposeful lives and filling their lives with meaning. Human beings feel lost when things that seem important are missing from their lives. Machines do not. They may recognize that things are missing as a fact, but they do not have any sort of emotional response to it.

Saying that, as a human being, you are not a machine may sound like a cliché. But it is really unfortunate when you look at how often human beings are treated as machines.

As a human being, it may often be up to you to speak up and say, "Treat me as a human, not as a machine."

item.title: Why Gratitude Sometimes Backfires
item.description:
Gratitude

Why Gratitude Sometimes Backfires

What if the best part of gratitude isn't feeling it?

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Gratitude is more complicated than Hallmark cards suggest, bringing both feelings of warmth and indebtedness.
  • In one experiment, gratitude reflection heightened stress reactions and reduced willingness to help.
  • Expressing gratitude directly to someone may leave us feeling more connected and supported.
  • The thank-you you're hesitant to share may mean more to the recipient than you expect.
Source: RDNE Stock project / Pexels

You can appreciate the people in your life and still dread being asked to announce it over dinner.

The turkey is carved. The cranberry sauce has made its annual appearance in the shape of the can it came from. Then someone says: “Let’s go around the table and say what we’re grateful for.”

Forks pause midair. Eyes drift toward the mashed potatoes like they might offer an escape.

A cousin says something heartfelt and beautiful, and now the emotional bar has been raised to Olympic height.

Am I grateful enough? Should I say something profound?

Gratitude rituals are meant to create warmth. And often they do. But psychologically, gratitude is a little more complicated than the greeting cards suggest.

The Emotional Fine Print

The benefits are real. A 2023 meta-analysis of 25 randomized controlled trials involving 6,745 participants found that expressing gratitude reliably improved happiness, life satisfaction, and psychological well-being compared with neutral activities.

But that doesn’t tell us everything about how gratitude feels in the moment.

In three experiments, psychologists examined people’s feelings after exercises such as recalling another person’s kindness or writing a gratitude letter they never sent. Alongside feeling moved and uplifted, the gratitude participants tended to report more indebtedness (and sometimes more feelings of guilt) than participants who did a neutral task.

It's like unwrapping a gift and realizing you didn’t bring one.

Gratitude can feel uplifting and slightly uncomfortable at the same time. It can carry a kind of social math: They gave + I received = Now I owe them

That discomfort doesn’t necessarily mean something has gone wrong. Wanting to give something back can be part of caring for a relationship.

But if gratitude can make us feel both good and uncomfortable, what happens when the discomfort arrives from somewhere else entirely?

The Cold Side of Gratitude

In a randomized study of 156 undergraduates, participants completed about 12 minutes of gratitude practice, mindful breath awareness, loving-kindness, or a neutral visualization exercise. Those who practiced gratitude did report more positive emotion.

But then researchers introduced a stressor: Participants had to submerge their hand in a bucket of ice-cold water while a researcher in a lab coat stood nearby, observing with the emotional warmth of a marble statue — which is exactly as pleasant as it sounds.

Under that stress, the gratitude group actually became the most emotionally reactive, reporting more negative emotion than any of the other groups. And of the four groups, they were also the least likely to donate time to help others afterward.

Not exactly a Hallmark-card ending.

Give Your Gratitude Somewhere to Go

Does this mean we should cancel giving thanks? Of course not.

Gratitude strengthens relationships and reinforces others’ kindness. But there's a difference between privately reflecting on gratitude and sharing it.

Privately reflecting on someone's kindness can leave us with an emotional mix: appreciation, plus obligation. Expressing gratitude may not make those complicated feelings disappear. But it can offer something more: connection.

A study of 916 students compared four approaches: writing gratitude letters they never sent, sending personal thank-you texts, posting gratitude publicly on social media, or just tracking daily activities. Participants repeated their assigned activity four times over about a week. Those who sent personal thank-you texts showed the strongest gains in feeling connected to and supported by others.

The takeaway isn't that texting is magical. It's that gratitude may do more to strengthen feelings of being connected and supported when we share it directly with the person we're grateful for rather than keeping it to ourselves.

And it may mean more to that person than we realize. In experiments by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, people expressing gratitude underestimated how positive recipients would feel and overestimated how awkward they would feel.

The thank-you you’re second-guessing may land more warmly than you expect.

A Gratitude Micropractice: Pass the Thanks

In my book, Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, I explore in greater depth how to practice gratitude without getting caught in feelings of indebtedness, and how to weave more appreciation, connection, and joy into the moments you already have.

Here’s one small place to start.

This Thanksgiving, when you feel gratitude for someone, try expressing it to them. Here’s a simple trick: Put a “you” in the sentence.

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my family," try, “Mom, you’ve always made people feel at home, even when the turkey’s running late.”

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my friends," try, "Noor, you’re the person I call when life gets messy, and somehow you always have a way of making it lighter.”

One describes what matters to you. The other lets someone know they matter.

Gratitude isn’t just noticing goodness. It’s letting someone know they helped create it.

This Thanksgiving, don’t just count your blessings. Let your blessings know they’re counted.

item.title: Are You Experienced?
item.description:
Philosophy

Are You Experienced?

Any discussion of experience depends on what exactly we mean by the word.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Experiences can be had or they can be made.
  • Experience is essential to epistemology (i.e., ways of knowing).
  • Lived experience is lovely but of limited use.

I must achieve internal consistency. —Edmund Husserl, turning an Erlebnis (Type I experience) into an Erfahrung (Type II experience)

The gods decreed that I shall not be a translator, and I am grateful for that. A direct translation from one language to another is a goal we can strive for, but rarely attain fully. The words of any particular language are rich in unique shades of meaning, allusions, emotional undertones, and cross-references to synonyms, which live lives of their own.

Homer called his hero Odysseus πολύτροπος (polytropos), literally “a man of many turns.” But being “of many turns” does not call forth useful associations in English, and so translators have struggled with—and argued with each other about—what to make of polytropos. Some render the idea as “endlessly cunning” (Mitchell, 2014), while others prefer “complicated” (Wilson, 2018). Neither hits the mark. One might as well try shrewd, crafty, clever, or inventive. “Endlessly cunning” is marred by the addition of the adverb, and “complicated” makes it sound like Odysseus needs therapy. “Complex” would have been a better choice. I prefer the phrase “a man of many devices” (Murray, 1919), which recognizes Odysseus’s rich and variable toolbox of survival skills, including those involving deception.

Different languages emphasize and elaborate different concepts, whatever is important in their natural and cultural context. We can marvel at some of these differences. Since Franz Boas (1911) suggested the Greenland Inuit have four different words for snow, others have grown the list, while still others have declared Boas’s observation a myth, one they find vexingly persistent. Other inter-language differences are less controversial, and some of these refer to psychological states. How many types of love are there? The Hebrew tradition counts four. What kinds of longing are there? Is the Portuguese saudade equivalent to the German Sehnsucht? On Seinfeld, Kramer asks George if he has ever yearned. “Yearned?” George replies. “I’ve craved!”

Psychological Science...

Psychology can be understood as the science of behavior and experience. Both terms carry complexity, and the latter more so than the former. What, we ask, is an experience? It does not take a Ludwig Wittgenstein to see that this concept embraces many variants that may not even share a single common feature. To say that an experience is whatever one experiences is to kick the can down the road; it is a tautology.

Source: J. I. Krueger, using Claude AI

When I asked A.I. Claude what an experience is, I received this response: “Experience (noun) has two main senses, and the difference matters.” Claude goes on to explain that one of these senses refers to a process or event, with a first-person involvement. A first kiss delivers this kind of experience. Another sense refers to accumulated knowledge or skill; the sort of thing you put on your résumé. The first sense is what is sometimes called lived experience, whereas the second sense goes further by demanding that something has been learned, something that contributes to the person’s σωφροσύνη (sophrosyne), or practical wisdom. Anyone can have a store of Type I (lived) experiences, but this does not make them “experienced.” The participle must be earned. To have lived experience may simply mean that one hasn’t died yet. To have Type II (empirical) experience means to have made active investments in life that can be cashed out to help reach one’s goals and enhance one’s well-being.

Explaining the conceptual difference between Type I and Type II experience in English requires space, patience, and some circumlocution. The German language offers a clean distinction between Erlebnis, ɛɐˈleːpnɪs, and Erfahrung, ɛɐ̯ˈfaːʁʊŋ. The difference between the two was elaborated by the philosophers Wilhelm Dilthey (1883) and Edmund Husserl (1900-1901), whose work is interesting to consider in light of today’s debates over epistemology (Krueger, 2026). Expressing a popular view, Aziz and Anjum (2025) suggest that the prevailing scientific ethos in psychology is limited and systematically biased by excluding, misrepresenting, and disadvantaging many human populations. What is silenced, according to this view, are the lived experiences existing in these populations. These lived experiences, it is further argued, must be given their due; they must be heard and respected. And so, the argument goes on, these lived experiences must be acknowledged as an alternative epistemology, a way of knowing things, a way of having “knowledges.” Authors arguing the line pursued by Aziz and Anjum differ in how far they wish to go. Some are willing to settle for a lived-experience epistemology being accepted as equivalent to the scientific theory-and-data epistemology. Others wish to see psychological science be remade in light of lived experiences. These writers view the traditional scientific epistemology as oppressive, colonialist, and exploitative.

Dilthey and Husserl would pause here. To them, Erlebnis (Experience Type I) and Erfahrung (Experience Type II) are equally essential to the human condition; they cannot be pitted against each other. What contemporary critics of conventional empirical science seem to miss is that Erlebnis cannot absorb Erfahrung. Being effortful, empirical, and hard-won, Erfahrung is the grounds for reasoned beliefs that can be put to the test, that can be modified or overturned by continued activity. Erfahrung remains a work in progress. An Erlebnis, by contrast, is registered, perhaps committed to memory, and then gradually lost. A tourist has Erlebnisse; a traveler gathers Erfahrungen. It is the difference between perception and cognition.

Science is Erfahrung tamed, structured, and refined into a systematic method. Well-designed studies are efficient ways of learning Nature’s secrets. We can have an Erlebnis when walking into the woods, but only by planting a garden, by experimenting with different seeds, and by pruning excess growth, can we come to have the kind of Erfahrung that allows us to explain things and to teach what we have learned. The rejection of science from the lived-experience perspective is a short-sighted endeavor. The most it can hope to achieve is a narrative. Listening to these narratives can be an Erlebnis, but what can it teach us?

Or myth?

Once the difference between the two types of experience is understood, many familiar narratives appear in a new light. An ancient myth tells us that Adam and Eve had lovely Erlebnisse in the Garden of Eden. In the Land of Nod, they were forced to make Erfahrungen. With that, they became self-aware.

Note: The image above shows what Claude produced when asked to capture the concept of lived experience visually. The effort is interesting but not entirely satisfying since there are several dimensions (time, space, meaning) cross-cutting a scheme built on the idea of concentricity. I confirm that I never use AI to do my writing for me.

item.title: How to Prevent Arguments at Thanksgiving Dinner
item.description:
Family Dynamics

How to Prevent Arguments at Thanksgiving Dinner

Keeping the peace when a disagreement threatens to derail the day.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Prioritizing our relationships matters more than proving a point or getting everyone to agree.
  • Interrupting the pace, not the people, can keep a heated conversation from turning into an argument.
  • Revisiting a sensitive subject may be someone’s way of processing something or longing to be heard.

The days leading up to Thanksgiving can feel like a whirlwind. Between figuring out who’s bringing what and dodging holiday traffic, nerves can wear thin before the first guest arrives. The extra leaf has to be wrestled out of the closet to stretch the table a little longer, and someone has been up since dawn coaxing the turkey toward golden. By the time everyone sits down, the coats are piled high on a bed down the hall and someone is sneaking a roll before grace. Then, somewhere between the first helping and the pie, a loaded remark cuts across the table and the tension becomes palpable. We spend weeks preparing the meal, yet the conversations shared over it rarely receive the same forethought.

Over the years, journalists have asked me how to keep Thanksgiving conversations from boiling over, and I always say we can’t control what others say or do, but we can choose how we respond. The key is remembering the person across the table matters more than proving a point.

Prepare for the Conversations, Not Just the Meal

Before the gathering, it helps to take an inventory of ourselves. I think of it like packing for a trip somewhere new. We check the forecast and pack for the weather we expect, knowing the skies can still shift once we land. In the same way, we can reflect on which topics might feel sensitive this year.

If some relatives tend to bring up challenging subjects, a quick heads-up can make those conversations easier to navigate. We might say, “I’ve been looking forward to being together, and it would mean a lot if we could keep things lighter this year.” Sharing this means everyone can arrive on the same page and enjoy one another’s company.

Pause Before We Respond

Thanksgiving conversations have a way of wandering into topics no one meant to open. A comment lands the wrong way and suddenly we’re deciding whether to let it go or respond. A racing heart can be a cue to take a breath and pause. In that pause, we can ask ourselves three questions:

Does this need to be said?

Does this need to be said right now?

Does this need to be said by me?

These questions can help us decide how, if at all, to engage. If the answer to any of them is no, we can steer the conversation toward common ground. We don’t have to follow every conversation into the weeds. Sometimes the kindest thing we can do for a conversation is to decide not to have it.

Not Every Disagreement Needs a Winner

At the same time, steering clear of hard topics isn’t always the answer. A difficult conversation doesn’t have to strain our relationships. Research on Thanksgiving discussions suggests that college students whose families encouraged open conversation reported more positive effects on family closeness and less stress afterward.

A disagreement does not have to become an argument. Much depends on whether we are trying to prove a point or to understand someone. Scholarship on serial arguments indicates that people often care more about working things out together than gaining the upper hand. Arguments tend to take hold once difference feels like a threat, pulling us into an either/or mindset where one view must prevail over the other. To stay on the side of understanding, we can ask ourselves, “How can I express my views while still showing respect and valuing this person?” If a conversation feels uncomfortable, we might say, “I hear you, and I hold a different perspective.” Sentiments like these help others feel heard, even when we see things differently.

Sometimes People Are Processing More Than We Realize

Of course, it wouldn’t be Thanksgiving without someone bringing up that topic—the one half the family has been hoping to avoid. We try to change the subject, and for a few minutes the conversation moves on to football and Black Friday deals. Then, just as everyone relaxes, that same relative finds a way back to the topic. It’s understandable to feel frustrated, yet shutting down the conversation can create more distance. After all, this is someone who matters to us, and there may be something more going on beneath the surface.

Difficult conversations can be complex webs of unspoken needs and hidden emotions. Maybe our relative is trying to make sense of something they’re going through, or looking for connection without knowing how to express that need. They may feel anxious or unheard. Or, there may be reasons we haven’t considered at all.

Without fully knowing the reason, some thoughtfulness can go a long way. It’s worth considering the experiences that may be influencing their viewpoint. Stepping into another’s shoes, even for a moment, can foster understanding and empathy. Offered sincerely, an affirmation such as “I can tell how much you care about this” conveys they are seen and heard, which can change the tone of the whole conversation.

Interrupt the Pace, Not the People

Other times, we watch from the sidelines as two relatives barrel toward an argument we all saw coming. Family arguments often gain momentum through the quick volley of replies, each one arriving a little faster and a little louder than the last. Before long, the momentum takes over in ways the original comment never would have on its own.

In situations like these, we can interrupt the pace, not the people. A calm invitation such as “This feels a little tense. Maybe we can pause this for now” can slow things down, and families tend to respond more openly to understanding than to judgment. Asking a relative to help carry dishes to the kitchen or check on the pie breaks the rhythm without putting anyone on the spot, giving each person a graceful way to step back with their dignity intact. The goal isn’t to referee or get everyone to agree, but to give the whole table a chance to reset.

Making Peace With Our Differences

Keeping the peace at Thanksgiving doesn’t require everyone to share the same point of view, and understanding someone else’s doesn’t mean giving up our own. We can, however, choose how we treat one another, even when we disagree.

item.title: With Age Comes a Unique Ability to Harness the Power of AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

With Age Comes a Unique Ability to Harness the Power of AI

Experience-based prompt engineering may be the ultimate AI hack.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Despite its great potential, AI can be intimidating, especially for older adults.
  • Perhaps surprisingly so, older adults possess an advantage in managing AI that many younger adults may not.
  • Prompt engineering based upon acquired knowledge and lived experience may be a powerful AI hack.
Source: geralt/ Pixabay

Co-authored by George S. Everly, Jr., PhD, MA, ABPP, and Barry McGovern, Solutions Engineer, JBS International

Today, November 19, 2026, is an important day in the world of artificial intelligence (AI). Anthropic, a major artificial intelligence company, is beginning to sell ownership shares of stock in the company to the public. At the same time, Anthropic’s founder, Dario Amodei, issued a warning. He cautioned that AI is developing more rapidly than expected, especially through the process of recursive self-improvement, which allows the programs to improve themselves without human guidance.

We often look to younger generations when it comes to guidance regarding AI. Perhaps surprisingly, older generations may have much to offer in managing and directing AI, especially at the level of personal use. Decades of lived experience, pattern recognition, and knowing how to ask the right questions allow older generations to harness the power of AI through the process of “prompt engineering” in a way that is more mature and experience-informed than it is for younger generations.

On average, older adults (age 50 or older) are more skeptical of artificial intelligence (AI), less trusting of its responses to questions, and less likely to use it than younger adults. While caution is warranted, older adults possess a hidden “superpower” in the form of prompt engineering based upon lived experience that, at least at this point, allows them to become active managers of AI rather than non-critical users, overly cautious passive recipients, or worse yet, non-participants. Ironically, this “superpower” is more prevalent in older adults than younger adults and may increase to some degree with age.

Use of AI Is Age-Related

For adults aged 18-40, the use of AI is likely 70 percent or higher. However, survey research conducted by AARP (AARP, September 23, 2025) found that familiarity with and use of AI decrease with age. About 47 percent of adults in their 50s reported knowing about and using AI, compared with 25 percent of those over 70.

In general, “Older adults are hesitant to adopt AI…in part, because of concerns over privacy, misinformation, security, and job displacement.” AI has shown propensities for biased reporting of data and a tendency to hallucinate, and it's perceived as mechanical. Consistent with Amodei's warnings, older adults believe AI is advancing faster than ethical and functional guardrails are being implemented.

The Risk of Passive Consumption

As described in a previous post, AI may encourage passive, non-critical consumption of information. The risks of such passive consumption have yet to be fully determined, but AI may lead to the inhibition of critical thinking and the creation of a functional dependence. A recent TV commercial showed a character gleefully stating that she has difficulty thinking without AI. It is this very passivity that increases the risk of an untethered AI.

Younger users may seem to treat AI like an answer machine because they don't yet have the foundational knowledge to critically assess the validity of the information provided. Older adults, by contrast, have a built-in "lie-detector” from decades of career and life experience—in short, they know what a valid answer is supposed to look like and may be better positioned than younger adults to ask follow-up questions that can challenge AI.

The Superpower Instilled by Age: Active Synergy With AI

Francis Bacon once noted, “If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.” So far, the errors or “overzealousness” exhibited by AI appear to be related to the questions asked of it. The more vague or less structured the questions, and the more repetitive the questions posed to AI, the greater its tendency to try to anticipate the desired answer and to “please” the questioner by “hallucinating” and creating spurious evidence to support the desired conclusions even though incorrect. In addition, AI does not possess the ability to independently assess the validity of the data it retrieves nor its recombinant output. As such, it may provide misleading or erroneous information.

The aging process is often accompanied by the accumulation of insights, knowledge, and informative experiences. These attributes may reveal themselves as the “superpower” ability to formulate specific, targeted questions. Rather than fostering passive consumption, knowledge and experience can foster informed, active consumption. It fosters the potential for a complementary, if not synergistic, relationship with AI wherein the person formulates knowledge- and experience-informed questions that not only target the efforts of AI but can serve as a series of checks and balances through AI’s recombinant efforts to provide answers.

For instance, a younger, less experienced person might ask AI, "Write me a business plan" (passive, vague), while a 60-year-old might ask, "Construct a business plan that overcomes these three most common reasons new tech companies fail" (experience-driven, targeted). Or, the less experienced consultant might ask AI, “Write an independent contractor’s agreement” (vague, too general), as opposed to “Create an independent contractor’s agreement that ensures the ownership of my pre-existing intellectual property does not transfer as a work for hire” (very specific, anticipating potential confusion over ownership).

Socrates believed the highest form of wisdom arose from introspection and self-reflection. Just as he used questions to challenge his students to provide the best answers to the most pressing questions of his day, perhaps we can harness questions in the Socratic method to guide AI to provide us with the answers to the most pressing questions of our day.

item.title: The Hidden Toll of Caring for a Chronically Ill Pet
item.description:
Caregiving

The Hidden Toll of Caring for a Chronically Ill Pet

What the research says about the psychological toll of caring for a sick pet.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Pets are family members whose care is rarely socially acknowledged.
  • Pet caregiver burden is as real and measurable as human caregiving.
  • Social validation directly reduces psychological burden in pet caregivers.
  • The bond, not the prognosis, drives anticipatory grief in pet caregivers.
Caring for a sick pet is a full-time labour of love. Research says the toll it takes is real.
Source: Matthew Henry / Unsplash

Pet caregiver burden is the negative physical, psychological, social, and financial toll experienced by owners caring for chronically or seriously ill companion animals. The term is adapted directly from human caregiving literature, where it is well established, and it now has validated measurement scales specifically designed for pet owners.

Research has consistently shown that owners of chronically ill pets carry a burden equivalent in psychological impact to those caring for ill human family members (Frenzel et al., 2026). Yet the experience remains largely unrecognised by the people around them.

“For many of us, our animals are our children,” says Courtney Wennerstrom, a Certified Pet Loss Grief Specialist and Companion Animal End-of-Life Doula, and the host and creator of The Hardest Goodbye, a podcast on grief, healing, and the animals who change us. “We feel an enormous responsibility to do everything in our power to protect them and keep them comfortable. But that devotion can come at the expense of our own well-being. We sacrifice sleep, exercise, social connections, and sometimes even our own medical needs because caring for them takes precedence over everything else.”

Jordan Davis, founder of the Canine Stroke Foundation, cared for her Border Collie, Finley, through three strokes, physical therapy, and a cancer diagnosis across the final 14 months of his life. “In his last couple of weeks, his back legs would stop working for a few minutes during potty breaks,” she says. “I supported the back half of his body weight. My back and arms hurt, but I would never have let him fall.”

How Caring for a Sick Pet Affects Your Mental Health

Caring for a chronically ill pet affects mental health in ways that mirror the human caregiving experience: chronic stress, sleep disruption, financial strain, social withdrawal, and a specific form of anticipatory grief that begins long before any loss has occurred.

A study published in June 2026 in Frontiers in Veterinary Science measured caregiver burden in owners of dogs with chronic neurological conditions and compared them directly to owners of healthy dogs (Frenzel et al., 2026). Caregiver burden was higher among owners of neurologically impaired dogs. What was especially notable was the effect of the social dimension: Owners who received positive feedback about their dog’s condition reported lower burden scores. Validation was not just emotionally supportive, but clinically protective.

A 2025 study of 347 guardians of senior dogs contributed a finding that challenges our assumptions about what drives this burden (Mellor et al., 2025). Anticipatory grief was strongly associated with caregiver burden and emotional closeness to the dog, but it was not associated with the severity of the dog’s condition.

Wennerstrom describes the emotional texture of this period with precision. “Anticipatory bereavement asks us to do two seemingly contradictory things at once,” she says. “Remain fully present with our animals and cherish the time we have left, while simultaneously trying to prepare ourselves for a future without them. We’re navigating love, hope, fear, uncertainty, and grief, sometimes all in the same moment.”

There is also, she adds, the pressure of suddenly becoming a nurse without any medical training: “Caregivers find themselves managing complex medication schedules, dressing wounds, monitoring symptoms, and remaining constantly vigilant for signs of a medical emergency. They’re also making difficult medical decisions, often terrified of making a mistake that could cause additional suffering.”

Why Pet Caregiver Burden Goes Unrecognised

The term for grief that society does not generally recognise or validate is disenfranchised grief. It describes losses that fall outside what the world treats as legitimate mourning: the end of a relationship that was never acknowledged, the grief of a miscarriage, or the mourning of an estranged parent are just a few examples.

The anticipatory grief and caregiver burden that precede the death of a pet falls in this category for most people.

A 2025 qualitative study of 31 animal caregivers found three consistent themes (Cameron, 2025): the psychological toll of having their grief dismissed, the work of finding meaning during and after illness, and the healing that came from social recognition. The third theme was not incidental. People described being believed as restorative. Being told that what they were going through was real changed how they were able to cope.

Wennerstrom sees a pattern emerge among the people she supports: a gradual narrowing of the world. “As our animals become increasingly dependent on us, we stop making plans, decline invitations, and withdraw from activities we once enjoyed because we’re afraid to leave them alone,” she says. “Over time, that isolation can become profoundly debilitating.”

Davis experienced this directly. “Others said he was old and had lived a good life, as if that meant I should be ready to let go,” she says. “They saw his wobbly walk and assumed he was in terrible pain. He wasn’t. I wish people had commented on how well he was doing: that he had overcome so many obstacles and was still full of joy.”

What helped, she says, was someone finally putting a name to what she was going through: “Being told about caregiver burden made me feel less alone, and less like I was making too big a deal of everything.”

Davis's dog, Finley, suffered his first stroke in August 2025, and was subsequently misdiagnosed. When she researched what resources existed for owners in her situation, she found the field lacking and veterinary professionals often underprepared to support the psychological experience of caregivers. Finley passed away in October 2026, at age 14.

Davis describes his last year as structured entirely around his needs: stretching, massage, and balance work woven through every day, two rounds of medications, and short walks in which he led and she steadied him if he stumbled. “Emotionally, it started after Finley’s first stroke,” she says. “I worried constantly that he would have another and might not survive, and anticipatory grief made it heavier.” After his second stroke, the anxiety became physical. “My heart raced constantly, and any time I had to leave the house I was trying to hurry back to him.”

She founded the Canine Stroke Foundation as a response to that gap, and as a tribute. “The foundation exists because of him,” she says. “He was my inspiration. Because he was resilient and kept going, I knew I could keep going too.”

What Reduces Pet Caregiver Burden

The same research that documents the burden identifies what reduces it. Social validation from people in the caregiver’s life is the most consistently protective factor across studies. Positive acknowledgement from veterinary teams, addressing the caregiver’s experience alongside the animal's condition, lowers burden scores.

Wennerstrom encourages people to lean on community actively rather than allowing their world to contract. “If leaving your animal alone feels impossible, invite friends over for dinner, watch a movie together, or organize a game night,” she says. “We need opportunities to laugh, experience joy, and remember that our lives still exist beyond caregiving.”

She also advocates for caregivers to maintain their hobbies wherever possible. “Our psyches can only absorb so much emotional pain at once, and we need moments when we can quiet our minds and simply exist outside of our grief. Even 20 minutes spent doing something we enjoy can help us recharge.”

Her most important recommendation concerns end-of-life decisions. Wennerstrom urges families to assess not only the animal’s quality of life but their own. “When an animal is seriously ill and the demands of caregiving have become unsustainable despite efforts to find support, that reality may also factor into the difficult decision about whether euthanasia is the most compassionate path forward.”

Davis tracked Finley’s quality of life using dedicated tools, counting good days, good days with difficult moments, and harder days. When the balance shifted, she made the call. His regular vet came to their home. “He was on his bed with his head in my lap, listening to his song,” she says. “He was at total ease, and it was peaceful.”

If you are going through something similar, please consider reaching out to the resources linked in this post. To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Home for the Holidays? 4 Survival Tips
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Home for the Holidays? 4 Survival Tips

A guide to making pleasant memories while breaking bread this season.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Political topics are likely to come up during holiday gatherings, so it's best to be prepared.
  • While some relish fiery debates at the dinner table, others find conflict anxiety-provoking or irritating.
  • Survival tips include setting clear boundaries, giving up the notion of "winning," and really listening.
Source: Taylor Heery/Unsplash

Are you headed to a gathering of friends or family in the coming weeks? Here is a heads-up: A November 2026 survey of 538 people found that 8 out of 10 respondents anticipate that political differences will come up during holiday meals (The Conversation). Further, a meta-analysis controlling for various factors found that dinners involving folks with diverse political perspectives were shorter by 24 minutes than dinners with politically uniform ones (Frimer & Skitka, 2020). How exactly these meals ended 24 minutes earlier is unknown. Hopefully it wasn’t a food fight.

The bottom line? Many folks consider political talk at holiday meals anxiety-provoking, preferring to focus on bonding and nostalgia. And yet many still may feel it is important to “return fire” on political views they deem uninformed, misinformed, or downright harmful. Post-midterm elections, a meme circulating on social media suggests that you bring up politics at holiday dinners so you can save money on gift purchases this year. Alternatively, when first sitting down at the table, one could ask, “Are we sick of ‘winning’ yet?” If you love conflict during meals, saying these sorts of things is likely to spark it. If, however, you'd prefer to keep your gatherings calm, here are some tips to survive your get-togethers:

Set clear boundaries ahead of time. Decide beforehand the topics considered off-limits (for you or others to bring up). If folks insist that you engage with them on an off-limits subject, communicate your limits using a calm tone and then have a plan to step away should they persist. One option is to stand up and apologize for having to take a call, real or imaginary.

Forget about winning. When exchanges are conceptualized as sharing perspectives, it's easier to shift away from the idea that this is a high-stakes battle and that victory is a necessity. The goal could instead be civil conversation. Keep your eyes on that prize, no matter what Uncle Charlie says to provoke a reaction.

Adopt a curious stance. If an exchange on politics does happen, show strong interest in how the person came to the views they're expressing. If tension rises, acknowledge the difference briefly and steer back to food, shared memories, or helping out. The merits of pumpkin versus bourbon chocolate pecan pie can present a useful distraction.

Try listening. Intentional, active listening is an important skill, especially now in a world where people desperately seeking to be victors in verbal battles are simply preparing their next salvo rather than paying attention to what the other person is saying. Really listening sends a palpable message that the person we are speaking to matters.

In conclusion, people may not remember specific details of an exchange of political views later on, but they will likely recall how they felt while speaking with us, and this brings us back to the context of a holiday get-together. Warm memories are still possible if we permit our better angels to prevail. Please pass the bourbon chocolate pecan pie.

item.title: My Kid Wants to Play Grand Theft Auto. Now What?
item.description:
Adolescence

My Kid Wants to Play Grand Theft Auto. Now What?

Some guidance for parentson Grand Theft Auto.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Grand Theft Auto, a video game known for violent and misogynistic content, just released its latest version.
  • Parents often feel backed into a difficult spot about giving their consent to gaming.
  • There are legitimate reasons to prohibit adolescents from playing the game.
  • Parents who permit their children to play should monitor for signs of harm and be ready to respond.

For the last days, even weeks, millions of parents have been fielding the pleas from their adolescent, even pre-adolescent, children to buy and play what is likely to be the biggest video game release in history – Grand Theft Auto VI.

Overall, it's important to have a balanced perspective. We don't need to get apocalyptic about this release. For most people, GTA6 will be a relatively harmless diversion that will consume a monstrous amount of time and then fade out. The risk that playing this game will turn your overall well-adjusted teen into a murderer or drug dealer is very low. This game, and media in general, is not the primary driver of mental health problems in youth; that would still be the old standbys: genetics, trauma, and adverse child experiences—social drivers of health.

The release of this game to child development and mental health professions is similar to how Halloween is experienced by dentists. Everything about it feels wrong, but few youth will probably experience long-term harm.

That said, we should not be naïve or complacent about some of the real risks.

These come in two main categories. The first is what is sometimes called displacement, which basically refers to the sheer volume of hours that youth will choose to spend on this game rather than on something healthier. Video games, just like gambling, are addictive, so some people are just not going to be able to stop and that can interfere with sleeping, homework, or just about anything else.

The second area of concern is related to the game’s content. GTA6 has everything that might be contained in an R-rated movie including graphic violence, drug and alcohol use and trafficking, nudity, and profanity. So, really, the question if you are a parent wondering about buying the game or letting your child get the game is: Would you be comfortable giving them unlimited and unsupervised access to being immersed in an interactive R-rated movie? I’ve heard they tried to dial down the misogynistic content in this version. We’ll see.

Even if the game doesn’t make your child act violently, it will still be tough to push out the more aggressive and misogynistic thoughts that will be swirling around in their head. There is also the concern that excessive exposure to violent video games can desensitize youth to real world violence.

Of course, adolescents are different and individuals are going to react differently to playing the game. For many it will be a relatively harmless waste of time but for others there could be more serious consequences, and it is important to try and see how playing the game affects your individual child.

My specific tips for parents:

  • If you are the parent of an early or mid-teen and get asked to buy or permit the game, it is more than okay to respond with a definitive hell no and explain why.
  • If you are going to permit the playing of the game, consider spending some time watching it and talking about what you see. Pay attention to how embarrassed your kid is when you are watching the game; this might actually be a good sign that they understand how depraved the content is.
  • Set reasonable limits, especially related to playing on school nights.
  • Monitor for signs of addiction or for changes in their behavior.

Sometimes I wish I could be one of those cool adults who is totally chill with immersive content that glorifies violence and criminal behavior, but I guess I’m not. Good luck, parents.
