item.title: Psychological Richness: The Third Dimension of a Good Life
item.description:
Happiness

Psychological Richness: The Third Dimension of a Good Life

How to fully compose your own life.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • A good life isn’t just happiness and meaning; psychological richness adds a vital third dimension.
  • Like music, a life is made up of harmony (happiness), rhythm (meaning), and complexity (richness).
  • Difficult, frustrating experiences can tank happiness while deeply enriching our perspective.

Imagine two people sitting at a quiet neighbourhood wine bar on a Tuesday night.

One has spent the last five years carefully pruning their life into a low-friction masterpiece. A dependable job with Sunday meal prep, and a tight circle of friends with minimal drama.

The other has spent those same five years changing industries, moving apartments twice, taking a solo trip where their luggage got lost in a country whose language they didn't speak, and surviving a breakup that rearranged their entire worldview.

If you asked someone coming from a traditional psychology background who is winning at life, they would likely give you two ways to score it. For over 40 years, researchers have treated a “good life” as a debate between two competing ideals.

On the one side is happiness (i.e., hedonic well-being): a life defined by comfort, stability, positive emotions, and a relative absence of stress. On the other is meaning (i.e., eudaimonic well-being): a life built on purpose, routine, coherence, and contributing to something larger than yourself.

For many, those two ingredients describe a lot. Plenty of people genuinely thrive on straightforward, comfortable lives anchored in meaningful contributions.

But think about the difference between someone who flourishes in the steady, familiar rhythm of a small town versus someone who only feels fully awake amid the unpredictable friction of a big city. If your primary goal is comfort and coherence, keeping your life simple works.

Alas, that doesn’t describe everyone.

I have spent years trying to figure out why that two-door framework never fully made sense to me. Having things straightforward has never reliably led me to a long-term sense of “good.” Whenever my life becomes too predictable, too frictionless, or too cleanly resolved—when every week looks like a neatly organized calendar block—I don’t feel serene. I feel strangely flat.

It turns out there's a reason that type of restlessness doesn't fit neatly into the classic binary. Psychologist Shigehiro Oishi and colleagues have spent the past several years making the case that we have missed talking about a third dimension of a good life: psychological richness.

Oishi defines a psychologically rich life as one filled with diverse, interesting experiences that fundamentally shift one's perspective. Unlike happiness and meaning—which are predicted by personality traits like conscientiousness, agreeableness, and emotional stability, as well as a preference for familiarity and tradition—psychological richness is driven by openness to experience and curiosity. It’s why a bizarre detour on a whim or getting immersed in a dense literary novel can make some people feel deeply alive even if it has zero connection to a five-year plan.

In their paper, Oishi and Westgate refer to happiness, meaning, and psychological richness as three “paths” to a good life. Personally, I think calling them paths makes it sound like you have to stand at a fork in the road, pick one direction, and leave the others behind. To me, a more coherent way to understand how these three elements actually work together is through music.

If your life is an album unfolding over time, happiness is harmony. It’s the consonant, pleasant chords that feel warm and uplifting in the moment.

Meaning is the rhythm section. It’s the steady bass line and recurring beat that give pieces structure, direction, and momentum. If you only optimize for harmony and rhythm, you can write clean, catchy pop songs in 4/4 time and play them happily for decades.

But there’s also that third consideration of psychological richness: the structural complexity of the composition. It’s the odd time signature, the unexpected key change, the dissonant bridge that introduces tension and forces you to lean forward because the arrangement refuses to stay predictable.

Once you hear life as an album rather than a linear path, something counterintuitive clicks into place: miserable, frustrating, or unwanted experiences can still make a life deeply worthwhile.

In music, dissonance doesn’t have to be a mistake; it can be what gives a resolution its emotional weight. Research suggests that difficult or disruptive events—heavy workloads, culture shock, failed mountain-climbing attempts, or even recovering from a serious illness—routinely increase psychological richness even while actively tanking day-to-day happiness. When researchers analyzed New York Times obituaries, lives rated high in psychological richness were actually negatively correlated with perceived happiness. You don't have to sit with the ringing of a dissonant chord for it to make the rest of the track unforgettable.

An appetite for complexity doesn't just leave someone with interesting stories. The research suggests that people leading psychologically rich lives score significantly higher in cognitive complexity, specifically attributional complexity and holistic thinking, even after statistically controlling for baseline openness to experience.

Attributional complexity is the ability to hold multiple, competing explanations in your head at once, to see the invisible situational pressures, systemic context, and messy human contradictions driving someone’s behaviour. Holistic thinking is hearing how the entire arrangement fits together rather than isolating a single note.

That's why low-complexity thinkers aren't drawn to psychological richness. When someone cuts them off in traffic, or ghosts them after three great dates, or makes a baffling career pivot, a low-complexity thinker reaches for a tidy, single-cause label.

Straightforward lives rarely ask your brain to stretch. When everything resolves cleanly on the downbeat, your brain gets to run on autopilot, relying on familiar scripts and neat categories. You stay comfortable, you stay coherent, but your worldview stops expanding.

I used to think my dissatisfaction with simple, linear progress meant I was bad at being content—or worse, that I was needlessly complicating a perfectly good groove. Framing it through psychological richness changes how I am able to reckon with these feelings.

Some people are built for a clean, consonant melody. There’s real beauty in that. But if you, like me, are wired for cognitive complexity, a life without friction, surprise, and perspective shifts won't feel like peace. It will feel under-composed.

When harmony, rhythm, and complexity all show up in the same piece, it can feel like magic. But if your life feels less like a tidy, predictable tune and more like an intricate arrangement you’re still learning how to play, it doesn’t have to mean you’re failing at living the good life.

It just means that you’re writing a song that is deeply your own.

item.title: Worried About Your Drinking? How to Cut Down, Comfortably
item.description:
Addiction

Worried About Your Drinking? How to Cut Down, Comfortably

Many of us drink too much without understanding why we depend on alcohol.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • If you drink too much, it's important to understand why addictive processes can take hold.
  • This brain-based process is the same, whether we rely on alcohol, comfort foods, or excessive screen time.
  • Understanding how these activities help numb, avoid, or distract from our feelings is key to reducing them.
Source: Joao Vitor Marcilio/Unsplash

How is your relationship with alcohol? Do you feel like you drink too much, perhaps vowing to cut down but slipping back into uncomfortable but familiar patterns? Many of us do. And that's hard, because alcohol is a socially acceptable drug, especially in Western societies. In the UK, you can buy it in supermarkets, grocery shops on every corner, in pubs, restaurants, and cafés. If you go to a party, alcohol is served. Or at dinner, people keep topping up your glass.

Alcohol is ubiquitous and hard to consume healthily, even with the best of intentions. Even if you're not alcohol-dependent, you may be uncomfortable about the amount you consume, but feel powerless to change that. Unfortunately, numerous studies show that regular drinking can have a major impact on your health, contributing to diseases including cancer, cardiovascular disease, dementia, and gastrointestinal diseases. It's clear that, in an ideal world, sobriety is the healthiest choice we can make. And if you do enjoy a glass of wine or beer, drinking in moderation is the next best option.

Understanding Why You Drink

If you would like to cut down, the first step is to understand why you drink too much. Let's start with the fact that alcohol tastes and feels good. If you've had a long day, a glass or two of wine helps you relax, gives you a warm, fuzzy feeling, and helps you transition from work to downtime. These transitions can be tricky for us, and we may use substances to help—for example, the morning coffee that provides the energy boost we need to transition from sleepiness to an alert, ready-to-work mode.

So, like other oft-consumed substances, alcohol feels good and helps us transition from one state to another. Another factor in our alcohol consumption is peer pressure. In my country, this starts as a teenager, when friends encourage you to drink excessively to be "cool" or "fun." This pressure continues at university, where heavy drinking is often socially sanctioned and encouraged.

Even in middle age and later years, having a beer in pubs or half a bottle of wine with dinner is seen as normal and desirable. Opting not to drink, although more and more common, can be tricky if your friends are on the boozier side. Although sobriety is increasingly embraced by the younger generation, people of my age (approaching 60) have grown up with alcohol, and opting for sobriety, or occasional drinking, is an effortful, often socially frowned-upon choice.

Which Part of You Wants to Drink?

Viewed through an internal family systems (IFS) lens, there is another pressure to drink, coming from inside your head. In IFS, drinking to excess, or in any way compulsively, is due to the actions of a protective part known as a "firefighter." This part's sole purpose is to extinguish the flames of pain that another—young, vulnerable—part might be struggling with. Firefighters are reactive and impulsive and have no sense of consequences—if you drink a whole bottle of wine, you may feel awful in the morning, but if it helps you feel less stressed, anxious, or lonely in the moment, the part's work is done.

Although the strategy of these firefighting parts can be terrible (they are also the parts that get people addicted to opioids, use pornography, gamble, and do all kinds of risky, self-destructive behaviour), they mean well. This cycle—a hurt, young part getting triggered and a protector urgently getting rid of the pain—is called an "addictive process" in IFS. And the same basic process applies, whether you are using substances or activities to numb, avoid, or distract yourself from painful feelings.

This can be hard to understand, so let's use Grace* as an example. Grace was a middle-aged white woman who came to see me for help with her drinking. She was a successful marketing executive with a young family, so she could ill afford the regular hangovers that blighted her life. "Every Monday morning I wake up with a pounding headache and a cold sweat," she told me in our first session. "I always overdo it on Sunday nights, because I'm so stressed out about going back to work. Then it's a bottle or more of wine, which helps me de-stress but of course makes the next day a nightmare."

One of our early tasks was to translate Grace's suffering into parts language. I explained that she had a young part, Little Grace, who found her high-pressure job extremely stressful. We later learned that it also triggered memories of being under intense pressure from her high-flying, academic parents, making school and exams hellish for her. When this stressed little girl got triggered by the mammoth to-do list waiting for her on Monday morning, a firefighter stepped in to wash away all that stress with way too much Chardonnay.

Finding Moderation

One of the many ways in which IFS requires a paradigm shift from other therapies is that, in order to help Grace drink in moderation, we had to work with the wine-drinking firefighter, not try to get rid of it (the well-meaning approach of 12-step programmes). When I spoke to this part, I learned that it had developed when Grace was a child, getting her to eat sweets and zone out in front of the TV after a day of grinding through her studies, while Grace's parents criticised her harshly for any mistakes. This showed us that, like all protective parts, this one meant well, even if it was causing chaos in her life.

We got permission from the firefighter to help Little Grace, which we did using IFS's "healing steps"—a roadmap for connecting with, comforting, and ultimately healing hurt young parts like this. We transported her from the past to live with adult Grace in the present, joining her loving, rambunctious family, which made her very happy. Only then could we work with the firefighter on changing their approach, which they gladly did. After much debate about becoming entirely sober or cutting down, Grace chose the latter, so we came up with a plan to only drink on Friday and Saturday with dinner, and nothing on Sunday or during the week.

Because all her parts had bought into this strategy, Grace could stick to it with relative ease, unlike the get sober/relapse/get sober again cycle common to many models for treating addiction. She ended therapy feeling optimistic about her future and with all the skills she needed to keep checking in on both Little Grace and the drinking part, to make sure they were OK, especially when she had a wobble and felt like slipping back into her old patterns.

I hope that's helpful for you. If you are struggling with your drinking, or any other substance/activity that feels compulsive for you, please do seek help. It's always possible to heal early wounds and change these painkilling habits, so don't suffer in silence—life is too short to waste feeling bad about yourself and your choices.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

* All case studies in these posts are composites. I never tell the stories of real clients, as confidentiality is very important to me.

item.title: Talking to Youth About Online Gambling and Sports Betting
item.description:
Parenting

Talking to Youth About Online Gambling and Sports Betting

How to broach the topic of online gambling with adolescents.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Adolescents are exposed to multiple forms of online gambling, from prediction markets to loot boxes.
  • It is important for parents to broach the topic of gambling with their adolescents.
  • Rather than using fear tactics, parents can provide accurate information about online gambling and its risks.
  • The goal is to open the lines of communication to encourage ongoing conversations about risk behaviors.

The gambling landscape has changed dramatically over a short period of time. Prediction markets (with a minimum age of 18), sports betting (complete with micro-bets), fantasy sports betting, iCasinos, and gambling activities within video games make gambling more accessible and more convenient than ever before. Indeed, online gambling “allows continuous and immediate access to gambling from virtually anywhere” (Forrest et al., 2026).

Adolescents have likely been exposed to online gambling in more ways than their parents might expect. Therefore, it is important for parents/caregivers to broach this topic to dispel myths about gambling, present accurate information about potential risks, and offer guidance. For parents who are unfamiliar with the online gambling landscape, here is a quick overview:

  • iCasinos: online casino games (e.g., poker, roulette, slots), which are often operated by illegal websites (though they are legal in a few states)
  • Traditional sports betting: betting on the outcome of a sporting event or making in-game bets (called micro-betting)
  • Fantasy sports betting: creating a fantasy team/roster and earning points based on the real performance of players (can be season-long or daily)
  • Prediction markets: “trading” on the outcome of future events (called contracts) such as the popularity of a show on Netflix, sporting events, oil prices, the weather, and various aspects of pop culture
  • Gambling activities in games: gambling within internet games such as purchasing loot boxes (which contain randomized rewards), skin gambling (i.e., gambling virtual cosmetic items on third-party websites), or betting on eSport tournaments

These online gambling activities may be particularly appealing to youth due to many factors, including ease of access, privacy, heavy marketing, celebrity endorsements, promotional incentives, constant action, unlimited opportunities to bet/gamble, loyalty programs, use of digital currency, normalization among peers, and stimulating sites/apps.

Starting the Conversation

Parents can find ways to bring up online gambling and sports betting with youth by referencing something they read online (like this blog post!) or after watching a commercial for a gambling app on TV. A few example questions parents could ask include:

  • “What have you heard about prediction markets?”
  • “How common is sports betting at your school?”
  • “How many of your friends buy loot boxes when they game?”
  • “Have you ever played fantasy sports?”

Once the conversation has begun, it is important for parents to listen with curiosity and care. Rather than using fear tactics, parents can provide accurate information about online gambling and sports betting to help adolescents understand the potential risks. It may be helpful to share essential facts:

  • Gambling activates the reward circuitry in the brain, which is the same region activated by drugs of abuse (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2013; Potenza, 2014). Gambling is designed to be reinforcing and stimulating to keep users engaged.
  • A portion of those who gamble develop gambling addiction (APA, 2013)—and it is not just those who go to casinos. The World Health Organization (WHO, 2019) now categorizes gambling disorder as (a) predominantly offline or (b) predominantly online. Both conditions are marked by impaired control over the behavior, increased importance of gambling in the person’s life, continuing to gamble despite negative consequences, and impaired functioning (WHO, 2019).
  • Gambling is not a way to “earn quick money”—gambling operators earn money when people lose (Nower et al., 2023). According to the American Gaming Association (AGA, 2026), the sports betting industry made $16.96 billion in 2025. They are not making that much money because people are winning.
  • Gambling problems/addiction are associated with several negative consequences such as financial issues (Nower et al., 2023; Oksanen et al., 2018), neglect of other important activities (e.g., schoolwork, relationships, hobbies), mental health concerns (e.g., depression, anxiety, suicidality (Moghaddam et al., 2015; Nower et al., 2018; Shaygan et al., 2024), academic problems (Arpaci et al., 2026), and isolation/loneliness (Arpaci et al., 2026; Shaygan et al., 2024).

Importantly, the goal is to facilitate a dialogue with youth, rather than having a one-way conversation. Parents can draw their adolescent into the conversation by asking: Why do they believe people are drawn to online gambling and sports betting? What are some myths they have heard about gambling? In what ways are gambling operators trying to make their products as enticing as possible? What might they do if a friend discloses that they have gotten into some trouble with gambling?

Finally, it is always helpful for parents to ask adolescents about their goals, short-term and long-term (e.g., what are their professional goals? Health-related goals? Financial goals? Spiritual goals?) and to explore their values. In this way, youth can recognize the discrepancy between their goals/values and gambling behaviors, and this recognition can serve as motivation not to engage (Miller & Rollnick, 2023).

Take the Risk

Parents may be hesitant to start this conversation with their adolescent due to the fear they won’t have all the answers or may not say all the “right things.” Yet, the goal is not for parents to use the perfect words; instead, the goal is to open the lines of communication to encourage ongoing conversations with adolescents about the risk behaviors they face today. Saying the right thing is less important than showing adolescents they care about their experiences and are available to talk and listen.

item.title: Feeling the Pain of Others
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Feeling the Pain of Others

Personal Perspective: When the work affects the individual.

Posted November 19, 2026

“Are you sure your work hasn’t gotten to you?” he asked. We were visiting our family in the Caribbean. We had hiked to the top of the cliffs on a small island, and for a moment the entire family stood quietly together, marveling at the sea. It was an exquisite sight—turquoise water as far as you could see, and a vast, cloudless sky. As we reached the edge of the cliffs, my first thought was, This is unbelievably beautiful. My second thought was, I wonder how many people have killed themselves by jumping off these cliffs.

I assumed everyone thought this; I asked my question out loud. My stepfather-in-law turned to me slowly and asked his question with such sincerity that I finally understood: My work had gotten to me. I didn’t even tell him the rest of my thoughts: Where would the helicopter land? Could it land on the beach, or would it land on this cliff and then they’d belay down? Is there even a Level 1 trauma center in the Caribbean? Would they have to go to Miami? Would they stop you in customs? It was quite a list.

I had always considered myself self-aware, but this was the first time I saw my work had transformed my engagement with the world.

Repeated Exposure to Others

My jobs had brought me into intimate contact with people who were living close to or experiencing different types of acute trauma. I worked in confidential locations and at large institutions. I worked days, evenings, and graveyard shifts. I worked in local communities, throughout the country, and the world.

Over time, friends, family, and even clients said I needed a vacation. Otherwise, stop taking everything so seriously. But I could not hear them; I was doing God’s work. They could either step up and help me or step off. I did not need to reflect on myself. I was arrogant, self-righteous, and impassioned, perhaps to the point of selective blindness. I was convinced that I was just fine.

After so many stories of abuse, death, and tragedies, including missing children, deported loved ones, climate disasters, and other nightmares, I had absorbed and accumulated other people’s pain to the point that it had become part of me, and my view of the world had changed. But I finally understood that this exposure to other people’s overwhelm had fundamentally changed me. I did the work for a long time with little ability to integrate my experiences emotionally, cognitively, physically, or spiritually. I suffered from compassion fatigue.

Rather than staying in touch with the heart that was breaking, I started building walls. In my case, this meant I became increasingly cocky. I had no access to humility, which we all need when honestly engaging our own internal process. Rather than acknowledge my own pain and helplessness in the face of things I could not control, I raged at the possible external causes. I sharpened my critique of systems and society. I became more dogmatic, opinionated, and intolerant of other people’s views. It never occurred to me that my anger might in part be functioning as a shield or that I was warding off anguish. A widely held belief: If you’re tough enough, cool enough, and committed enough, you’ll keep on keeping on. You’ll suck it up.

Instead, I began the long haul of making change. I acknowledged the effects of other people’s pain; I made room for my own internal process. Over the years, I gradually let go. This fatigue takes a personal and professional toll.

Honoring Suffering Without Taking It On

We are slow to recognize such fatigue as a broad social concern rather than an isolated individual issue—through a job, daily life, or caregiving. It also goes beyond exposure to human suffering; other species and the planet are also in pain.

I needed a new framework that allowed me to bear witness to suffering without surrendering my ability to live fully—I call the concept trauma stewardship. This refers to the entire conversation: How we are affected over time, how we make sense of, learn from, and ultimately transform, individually and collectively.

In stewardship, we are entrusted with people’s stories and lives, animals’ well-being, and our planet’s health. We understand that this is an honor as well as a responsibility. As stewards, we make room for and honor others’ hardship and suffering, yet we do not assume their pain as our own.

The essayist E. B. White once wrote that the early American author, naturalist, and philosopher Henry Thoreau had perhaps been “torn by two powerful and opposing drives—the desire to enjoy the world, and the urge to set the world straight.”

item.title: How to Cope With the Season of Family-Focus
item.description:
Infertility

How to Cope With the Season of Family-Focus

The year-end is hard when you're struggling to build your own family.

Posted November 19, 2026

November through New Year’s is marketed as the magical season, and for many people, it can be. But if you are struggling with infertility and/or pregnancy loss, it can represent two months of triggers, traumas, jealousy, and misery. Why? Lots of reasons.

Many people save surprise pregnancy announcements for gatherings, which can be agonizing for anyone who wants nothing more than to make such an announcement themselves. Family and friend parties bring forced encounters. Intrusive questions are common: So when are you going to start a family? I hear you’ve been struggling. I think you should see my cousin’s doctor. You need to gain weight, exercise less, try my herbalist, or just adopt.

And it doesn't help when the focus of TV specials, commercials, and religious services is on babies and children. What can you do to make this season a bit less dread-worthy? Maybe even experience some joy?

  • Prepare “snappy comeback lines” for intrusive questions.
  • You don’t have to hold babies or play with toddlers.
  • Memorize excuses—you’re coming down with a cold, you were exposed to a stomach bug, whatever works.
  • Avoid malls, parties, and religious services earlier in the day when more children are present (if this triggers you).
  • Volunteer for those less fortunate. This may help you feel better, and many agencies need volunteers.
  • Create escape plans if needed—signal your partner that it’s time to leave.
  • Plan how to get away from distressing situations or conversations. (Offer to wash dishes or wrap gifts, develop a new passion for watching football, or bring “work.”)
  • Don’t force yourself to go to a toy store to buy gifts for the children in the family. Order online, buy the books you loved as a kid, or give gift cards.
  • If being with family and friends feels like too much, don’t. You can book a trip, after all.
  • Create your own holiday traditions that bring you peace and pleasure.

Don’t assume that every pregnancy announcement or belly was achieved easily or through spontaneous sex (roughly 1 in every 37 babies are conceived through IVF). Many people never share their infertility struggles, and most of those who build their families through donor eggs, sperm, or embryo don’t tell anyone.

You are not alone. It is estimated that 1 in 6 individuals struggle with family-building.

If you can’t get into the holiday mood whatsoever, don’t pressure yourself. The majority of those experiencing infertility report symptoms of anxiety and depression, and women experience the same level of psychological distress as do women facing cancer or heart disease.

Most importantly, put yourself on your own list; nurture yourself.

item.title: Tips for Newly Divorced Co-Parents Around the Holidays
item.description:
Divorce

Tips for Newly Divorced Co-Parents Around the Holidays

The first holiday season after divorce can be the hardest.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • The first holiday season post-divorce can be the most challenging for you and your children.
  • Ensuring you and your co-parent are aligned is crucial.
  • As always, communication is key to smooth transitions and less anxiety for all.

As is true for many significant life changes, the first holidays after a divorce can be the most challenging as you and your new family unit navigate a new world.

This is particularly true when there are children involved. Divorce will affect the holiday season for all of you—which might mean changing many holiday traditions.

This may mean not having your children at your family’s traditional annual gathering or waking up on Christmas morning without your children.

As hard as that is to fathom, when making decisions about splitting the time, keep in mind it is reasonable for you to have one holiday and your co-parent to have the other. In addition, some of the greatest sources of pressure, particularly in a recently established separation or divorce, are issues related to custody.

Here are a few basic questions to consider as you embark on co-parenting through this sometimes anxiety-producing, emotional time of the year.

Who Gets the Children, and When?

If you are already divorced and have a settlement agreement that addresses this, refer to that document if you have questions regarding who has the children when, and for how long.

In my legal practice, I set out very specific provisions regarding the holidays, including who will have the children, when and where pick-up and drop-off will occur, and a requirement to share itineraries if the children are traveling with a parent. Typically, the “holidays” are alternated or divided by the parents.

If your agreement does not contain this level of detail, or if you are separated without any paperwork as of yet, it would be wise to reach out to your former or soon-to-be-ex spouse and discuss holiday plans so that everyone can make arrangements, and the children are not left wondering how they will be spending their holiday and vacation time.

How Do We Evenly Split the Time?

Keep in mind that it is reasonable for you to have one holiday, and your spouse, the other. Simply, if you get Thanksgiving, your spouse gets Christmas/Hanukkah/Kwanza, or whichever holidays are celebrated and whatever combination applies. With that said, many couples can be more flexible.

Sometimes, for example, one parent might have the children on Christmas Eve and the other on Christmas Day. Or, depending on how closely the parents live, they might agree to divide Thanksgiving in such a way that one parent has the children for the meal and the other for dessert. Or they might agree to split Thanksgiving weekend so that the children can travel to see both sets of grandparents.

There are seemingly countless ways to make these case-by-case arrangements, and each situation can be custom-fitted with a plan for the couple and their children’s needs. The critical issue here is that both parents must agree, and, ideally, you have that agreement in writing, preferably in a legally sound document, in the event that there is an unexpected change in point of view.

What if Co-Parents Do Everything “Right” and the Children Are Still Unhappy?

No matter how carefully and evenly you plan out your holiday arrangements, you might still face challenges regarding how the children respond to the first few holiday seasons when their parents are living in different homes.

I work with many therapists as part of my practice, and their consistent advice is to do everything you can to avoid conflict in front of your children, to not to speak ill of that parent in front of your children, and, whenever necessary, to do everything you can to put your children’s needs ahead of your own.

Your Children Need and Deserve Both Parents in Their Lives

While this entire experience can be gut-wrenching, it is important to remember that your ex-spouse is still your child’s parent, and, to be happy and healthy, children need to have access to both parents. Furthermore, each of you needs to have an opportunity to build new traditions with your children in a new family unit.

Most of all, it is critical to remember to protect your emotional well-being and the emotional health of your children during these stressful times.

Do everything you can to enjoy the holidays and ensure that your children do as well, particularly as you proceed through your divorce.

And as I always say, please take time out to take care of yourself during what can be an incredibly stressful time.

item.title: The Instant Ick: When You’re the Only One Who Sees the Hypocrisy
item.description:
Empathy

The Instant Ick: When You’re the Only One Who Sees the Hypocrisy

Empathy unhooks us from the reactive stance of disgust.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Inauthenticity can hide behind humility and perfection, not just arrogance.
  • Moral disgust is a protective, visceral reaction, and it shows on the face.
  • Empathy for others and for ourselves helps us find an authentic response.

Can you spot inauthenticity in a flash?

I don't mean the obvious kind, where someone needs to be better than everyone else. That kind is easy to feel. They talk a little louder, push a little harder, and take up more space than the moment calls for. Like a black hole, they absorb the energy in the room and give nothing back.

There is a quieter kind of inauthenticity that often goes unnoticed, because it arrives dressed in humility and perfection. You probably know the type: the person who can do no wrong, who seems to have a tender heart for everyone, and who is praised by all for being so good.

Two Routes to Status

Both kinds of inauthenticity are about status. Alfred Adler, one of the earliest psychologists to study power, observed that the striving for superiority can also take the form of a striving for perfection, or "godlikeness." Superiority usually plays out over worldly things, like success or winning an argument. Godlikeness plays out on a level ordinary mortals can never reach.

Those of us who are deeply connected to our own humanness often feel this second kind most keenly. When someone seems a little too pious or a little too perfect, we feel an instant ick. Some part of us knows they are hiding their human nature.

The Ick Has a Name

That reaction is moral disgust. Like physical disgust, it is visceral: a feeling of repulsion designed to protect us from what could harm us. It is why such people can be so hard to be around, and why we often feel an urgent need to tell someone what we saw. Disgust makes us pull away from what feels contaminated and reach for what feels clean and true.

The frustration is that few people believe us. To most, this person is a role model. We all want to overcome our weaknesses, and they seem to have done it.

There is another reason we may not be believed. Someone who has earned a reputation for being good, without paying the price of actually being good, is often on the lookout for signs they are about to be exposed. And moral disgust, like physical disgust, shows on the face. Research suggests it activates the same facial muscle we use when we taste something bitter: the upper lip rises and the nose wrinkles.

So they may work, quietly, to discredit the person who saw through them. A hint dropped here. A flicker of alarm there. All while appearing to be above it all. Nobody questions their intentions, precisely because they seem so good.

Suddenly you are the judgmental one. The difficult one. The one who needs to change.

The One-Two Punch

This is the one-two punch of hypocrisy: First you witness it, then you are made to pay for seeing it. It can shake your sense of self-worth, because we are social animals. As researchers Romin Tafarodi and William Swann Jr. write, "We cannot refrain from peering into the looking glass that others hold up to us, as much as we distrust the images we see there."

I have had my share of these experiences, and they have been especially painful because I care deeply about connection. I like being someone others can depend on, not because I need to feel valued, but because connection is part of what makes us human.

Empathy as a First Step

As I've grown older, I have tried to look past the hypocrisy. Behind the piety or perfection, there is often a frightened child who never felt acceptable as she was. The idealised image masks her pain, and she cannot afford to drop it.

Empathy is an important first step. It unhooks us from the reactive stance of disgust, and from its urge to make sure everyone else knows.

But empathy is neither an end in itself nor a one-way street. Used only outward, it can become spiritual bypassing: staying silent in the name of being a good person, even when bringing the hypocrisy to light would be important or healing. When we direct empathy toward ourselves, too, and toward our own hurt, it becomes a means to an end: finding the response that is right for us.

Finding Your Response

When we rest in a place where everything we feel is allowed, without labels or judgment, we begin to hear the inner voice that tells us how to respond. It isn't easy, but this is the work of authenticity: expanding our capacity to be with what is, and trusting the guidance that is always in conversation with the present moment.

Every situation is different, and no single answer fits them all. Sometimes hypocrisy needs to be named, especially when it is harming someone. Sometimes it is best left alone, especially when other people's relationships are involved. You might not tell your partner that their mother is a hypocrite, because it could shake their whole sense of self. Unless her hypocrisy is harming you, in which case you may need to raise it with kindness, or set boundaries that protect you.

No one can tell you what is right for you, because no one else is living your experience. But when you listen inward, you find not only the answer but the courage to act on it. You will need that courage. There are no guarantees. People may criticise you, and things may not go as planned. Yet trusting your inner guidance lets you look yourself in the mirror and say, "I did what felt right at the time."

Recognising inauthenticity is, in many ways, simply our wiring, designed to keep us safe from other people's hidden motives.

Responding authentically is power.

A Reflection to Try

Think of someone who gives you that instant ick. Notice where you feel it in your body, without judging yourself. Then ask: If I weren't triggered at all, what would I see? Perhaps a frightened child behind the mask. Perhaps someone causing real harm. From that place, what does the situation call for: letting it be, speaking up with kindness, or a boundary that protects you?

item.title: 8 Questions to Know If Your Relationship Is 'Fake Happy'
item.description:
Authenticity

8 Questions to Know If Your Relationship Is 'Fake Happy'

Authenticity in a relationship is not a given, it has to be built.

Posted November 19, 2026

Source: Nothing Ahead / Pexels

Relationships can be messy and complicated, yet they remain the most beautiful connections we can form. But what happens when a partner tells you to put on a happy face and to stay positive no matter what—suggesting that you sweep the mess under the rug? This is what psychologists refer to as “toxic positivity,” and it is more common in relationships than we’d like to admit, and detrimental, too.

Research is now unraveling why your authentic self is better than slapping on a fake smile, especially in your love life. In light of this, psychologists can now measure whether your relationship embraces authenticity.

Toxic Positivity and the Problem With Suppressing Emotions

In a study that investigated individuals’ awareness and acceptance of mental health issues, researchers explored the influence of toxic positivity—the societal pressure to pretend everything’s fine, even when it’s not—on well-being. According to the authors, “When we force our brain to be in a false state of wellness, we send a message to our brain that whatever the emotion is, it is in some way bad or dangerous.”

When we avoid emotional discomfort, we may unintentionally be making those feelings larger and more overwhelming in the back of our minds. Pushing down real emotions leaves a mark, and those feelings sneak up on you when you least expect. Avoiding emotional discomfort doesn’t make it disappear; it just amplifies it.

Embracing Authentic Emotions: The Authenticity in Relationships Scale

Relationships thrive on authenticity. Pretending everything’s perfect when it’s not can be like throwing fuel on the flames. Research consistently shows that being open about your feelings is key to a healthy and stable love life.

In light of this, research in Personality and Individual Differences aided the development of the Authenticity in Relationships Scale, a tool that measures how true to yourself and others you are in your social connections. The scale includes eight items to which respondents rate their level of agreement:

  1. I always hide my true thoughts for fear of others’ disapproval.
  2. I usually try to cater to others.
  3. I do not dare tell others the truth because I care for their feelings.
  4. I am never aware of when to insist on myself and when to compromise.
  5. I never find ways to reconcile my needs and those of others.
  6. I don’t always tell the truth without considering how others will think of me.
  7. I never speak my mind without taking care of others’ feelings first.
  8. I never offend people by speaking frankly.

Researchers have concluded that real-life couples who toss aside the “fake it till you make it” script report more satisfaction and resilience when the going gets tough. The developers of the scale found authenticity to predict higher levels of agency and communion within relationships, as well as greater subjective well-being at the individual level.

Open conversations, mutual respect, and a team mindset should always be the goal. Inauthenticity or toxic positivity, on the other hand, makes for a relationship filled with eye-rolling at genuine concerns, brushing off real issues, or pretending everything is sunshine and rainbows when it’s not.

Relationships flourish when we acknowledge and respect emotions authentically.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: How I Had to Learn to Stop Saying “Yes” When I Meant “No”
item.description:
Alcoholism

How I Had to Learn to Stop Saying “Yes” When I Meant “No”

Learning to say no can be an important part of changing your drinking.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Stopping drinking alone doesn't fix deep-rooted people-pleasing tendencies.
  • Learning to say no is a practiceable skill that supports lasting sobriety.
  • Many "drinking problems" are actually "drinking solutions" to deeper emotional conflicts.

For years, I was a girl who would say “yes” when I meant “no.” It was only after I decided to stop drinking that I realized how much my “yes-girl” tendency had fueled my drinking cycle over the years.

A Drinking Solution to a “Yes-Girl" Problem

Over the years, both through my own recovery and my work in helping others break their drinking patterns, I have come to see that most people who eventually come to question their relationship with alcohol don’t have a “drinking problem;” instead, they have a “drinking solution.” In my case, my inability and unwillingness to say “no” had created a lot of problems that I ended up turning to alcohol to solve.

I would say yes to a football weekend marathon when I didn’t even know what a quarterback was, and then turn to a 6-pack to make time pass faster. I would say “yes” to hosting the relative whom I couldn't stand, then try to push away my resentment with a bottle of wine. I would say “yes” to helping out at a neighbor’s garage sale after a long week and end up trying to recover from exhaustion with a few cocktails.

The Invisible Drinking Loop: The Yes-Effect Loop

The Invisible Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

As I started to help others break their old drinking patterns, I realized I was far from the only person who got caught in this pattern. In fact, I came to nickname this particular drinking pattern “the Yes-Effect Drinking Loop.” It’s one of the 10 most common invisible drinking loops that keep an unwanted drinking pattern alive.

In most unhealthy drinking patterns, drinking is only what we see on the surface. The Invisible Drinking Loop is a term I created to help people understand the hidden forces that keep their drinking patterns alive. An invisible drinking loop is often driven by the need to solve a problem, fueled by the belief that alcohol can help, and maintained by the habit loop in which drinking has become the default routine to cope with or deal with certain situations or emotions.

In the “Yes-Effect Drinking Loop,” drinking has become the solution to deal with the side effects that arise when a person struggles to say no.

Why Stopping Drinking Is Not Enough to Break the Loop

As is true with most drinking loops, simply stopping drinking doesn’t break the loop.

With alcohol out of my life, I found myself sitting through events that I had no interest in, battling the desire to reach for a drink to make time pass faster, hanging out with people whose company I didn’t enjoy, missing the quick mental escape alcohol could offer, and dealing with overwhelming cravings by the end of the day after I once again stretched myself too thin in the effort to please others instead of honoring my own limitations.

It took me a long time to realize that simply stopping drinking doesn’t solve the problems; instead, it exposes them. I needed to learn to find another way to address the problem that I once attempted to solve through drinking, and that meant learning how to say no.

The Mindset Upgrade: My Needs vs. Others’ Expectations

Learning to say no after years of saying yes is not easy. When faced with a choice between disappointing others and disappointing myself, my default response was to choose the latter. Somewhere along the line, I had been conditioned to believe that fulfilling others’ expectations, even those of people whom I wasn't even that close to, was a way to keep myself safe, liked, and in good standing.

Yet, I failed to see the hidden cost of all the efforts to keep others happy; I kept myself unhappy. So much so that alcohol became the only way I knew how to push down my disappointment, exhaustion, and resentment.

Learning to say “no” started with a radical decision to honor my own preferences rather than automatically prioritize others’ expectations. Don’t get me wrong, it doesn’t mean becoming self-centered or never making compromises in life. But it does mean taking an intentional pause before giving in to my compulsive need to keep others happy. And when faced with the choice between disappointing others and disappointing myself, I wanted to make that choice consciously, rather than by default.

The Skill Expansion: Learning to Say No

The 4-Pillar Sobriety System
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

Of course, giving myself permission to say no was one thing. Actually knowing how to say it was another. After years of automatically saying yes, saying no felt like a skill I had not yet learned.

That's why Skill Expansion is one of the core pillars of my approach to breaking an old drinking pattern. Truly growing beyond alcohol often requires us to develop new skills and tools to navigate the challenges we once relied on alcohol to handle. For the Yes-Effect Drinking Loop, learning to say no is one of those skills.

Fortunately, like most skills, saying no is something we can learn through practice. Personally, I've found that having a few ready-to-use ways to say no makes a world of difference. That's why I've put together 7 of my favorite scripts for saying no with grace.

item.title: Are Your Sons the Casualties of a Gender-Based Reading Crisis?
item.description:
Parenting

Are Your Sons the Casualties of a Gender-Based Reading Crisis?

These 4 Recommendations May Help

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Boys are significantly less motivated to read than girls.
  • The decline in boys’ motivation to read tracks closely with a decline in reading achievement.
  • Research on motivation to read can guide what parents do to foster the reading habit with their sons.

When British author Ian McEwan, one of my favorite storytellers, thinned out his home library of duplicates and extras to make room for new stock, he took boxes of books into the park next door and gave them away to passersby. To his surprise, the only ones accepting these gifts were women. He came away from this experience with the realization that if females ever give up on reading, this remarkable invention of human technology will surely die with them.

Thankfully, females have not yet turned their back on the printed page, but ominous trends in reading habits for girls and boys suggest that at least the level of enthusiasm for reading among both genders is in decline. And as motivation to read slips, so does reading skill.

Where this relationship is most pronounced, however, is with boys, who have significantly lower levels of reading engagement than their female counterparts and fall well short of girls in reading achievement on global, national, and state-level reading assessments. When it comes to enjoyment of reading, time spent reading for pleasure, and diversity of text read (i.e., newspapers, magazines, fiction, nonfiction) girls in the U.S. and in most countries of the world have significantly and consistently higher levels.

I’ve often discussed in my books on the topic of boys and reading, as well as in speeches and lectures at conferences, that for those of us with sophisticated literacy skills, we hope the same for the guys within our care. This is because we desire boys, and indeed all youth, to experience the joy and benefits of the type of highly developed literacy abilities that we value and that have in very real ways contributed to our personal enrichment and professional accomplishments. However, there’s no shortcut to getting there. We can’t expect boys who rarely read to ever possess the level of literacy we wish for them. Parents who accommodate their sons’ non-reading habits are in some ways enabling stunted literacy growth.

4 Recommendations for Keeping the Guys in Your Life Reading

Research tends to do a good job of documenting the decline in reading engagement and achievement without always specifying the causes. Thus, it’s helpful to look at the literature related to motivating students to read and then by inference appreciate the reasons for the lack of motivation. For example, researchers have discovered factors that positively influence motivation to read, such as (a) creating contexts for free self-selected reading, (b) giving students more text choices, and (c) structuring collaboration for reading and learning. Looked at from the opposite perspective, then, one can infer that students are disengaged when time is not set aside for free reading, when students’ choices about what to read are restricted or non-existent, and when students only read in isolation without opportunities to discuss and share texts.

These same lessons from research can help guide parents who are eager to create supportive environments for reading for their sons.

  1. Have an abundance and variety of reading material in the home. These books and texts should be related to your sons’ interests, desires, aspirations, and hobbies. Researchers have shown that a key factor in keeping children and youth reading, even during the summer, is the number of books in the home.
  2. Model reading for pleasure and information. In my own research for my books on the topic, I came upon numerous ingenious ways some dads and adult men are taking their reading role model responsibilities seriously. In one case, a program called Books and Balls involved little league baseball coaches who doubled as sponsors of book clubs with the players. A similar approach is a clever program called Kicking and Reading wherein professional and semi-professional soccer players teach boys on-field techniques and also read with the boys.
  3. Keep an open mind about what your son should read. A boy in my university reading clinic told us how his mother required him to read chapter books that he found boring and difficult. Slyly, he would slip comic books between the chapter book covers and read those instead. I’m not suggesting a diet made up solely of comic books is desirable, but setting too high a standard for the type of material a boy should read, especially a boy who is disinterested in and struggling with longer texts, may turn him off to reading entirely. I have written about how comic books and graphic novels can provide boys visual scaffolding to aid comprehension. And many have reached a level of sophistication both in terms of art and content to be a worthy part of boys’ recreational reading.
  4. Form a family book club. As members, sons should be allowed to contribute reading material to the club, whether a sports article, rap lyrics, a magic book, or graphic novel. I once interviewed a single mom who enticed her two sons to read by allowing them to skip after-dinner chores to participate in their book club. I have found that once the reading habit is established through book club participation, boys are willing to engage with and select lengthier and more complex texts.

I’m fond of saying at the conclusion of my talks on this subject that “A boy’s love of reading doesn’t begin with scholarship, it begins with discovery." The more we do to help boys discover or rediscover the joy and pleasure of reading, the greater the chances they’ll become engaged and skillful readers for life.

item.title: How to Recover From High School
item.description:
Adolescence

How to Recover From High School

What to do if high school was a real low for you.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • A 2025 YouGov survey found that 12 percent of respondents disliked high school while 8 percent hated it.
  • Recognize that high school was only four years and that you didn't get to choose your classmates.
  • Learn to forgive your classmates and your high-school self.
Source: Mian Rizwan / Pexels

High school may have been a high for many. But if it was a low for you, you ain't alone. A 2025 YouGov survey found that 12 percent of respondents disliked high school while 8 percent hated it. Consider me among the 8 percent.

Having a lot more "grrrrs" than "rah-rahs" in high school could leave you holding onto Rs—namely, resentment and regret—which could keep you trapped in your high-school days way longer than you'd want.

Here's how to truly graduate from all that:

Realize That in High School You Weren't With People You Chose

A friend once described high school as "The last time that you had no choice of who is going to be around you most of the time," because your high school totally depended on where your family happened to live and what resources and connections they happened to have. Therefore, chances were quite high that you were around high-schoolers who didn't fit very well with you.

My high school, for example, had very little diversity and was filled with people not used to dealing with those of different racial, ethnic, cultural, and socioeconomic backgrounds and ways of thinking. For example, my high-school soccer team had never seen someone like me play soccer. So, it was pretty common to hear racial stereotypes and epithets hurled around throughout my teenage years, making me feel quite alone.

Understand the Limitations of Your High-School Classmates

This brings up an age-old problem—or perhaps an age-young one. Your high-school classmates were in their mid-teens at the time. Their brains and senses of self were still developing like fruitcake batter that had just entered the oven. That, along with their lack of life experience, left them quite limited in their ability to process things around them, know right from wrong, and think for themselves. There are reasons why rental car companies have traditionally charged extra until you've passed your 25th birthday.

Does that guarantee that all of your high-school classmates will eventually grow out of their high-school selves? Of course not. Nevertheless, surely you wouldn't base your worth on what any teenager would say about you now? Heck, I wouldn't even listen to my own high-school self.

Forgive Your Classmates and Your High School Self

That's because I was still full of "Never Have I Evers" back then—way before I had actually traveled around the world, met a much greater diversity of people, developed real friendships, and engaged in real romantic relationships. For a while, it was hard to look back at my naive high-school self without a ton of cringe. But I have since learned to forgive my teenage self—recognizing that I didn't know better at the time.

Part of healing is forgiving your high-school classmates as well. For example, the female classmate who once told me, "You are smart and funny, so I like hanging out with you, but you are so incredibly ugly," probably wasn't used to seeing a diverse range of looks and people. Also, her frontal lobe may not yet have been developed enough to tell her, "OK, maybe don't say something like that if you want that person to help you with your homework or teach you how to play sports."

Recognize That High School Was Only a Tiny Fraction of Your Life

Of course, the fact that to save money my dad—rather than, you know, taking me to a real barber—would regularly cut my hair, leaving my head looking like that of a LEGO person, probably didn't help. But eventually you realize that you can recover from not only a bad haircut but also high school. After all, high school is only four years and not forever—lasting about as long as a pair of heavily distressed jeans.

Set Firm Boundaries Between You and Your High-School Years

It is important, though, to treat any distressing high-school experience like you would a pair of out-of-fashion distressed jeans. Throw them away so that they don't keep taking up space—space that you could otherwise use for new memories, experiences, people, and growth. In fact, get rid of anything that may trigger low high-school memories, such as severing ties with anyone who doesn't recognize that you have outgrown your high-school years. If you do find it difficult to move on from those years, get help from others, such as a professional therapist.

Realize That There Is Time to Rebuild Yourself and Your Social Life

You'll need to free up that mental and emotional space because you may have a lot of catch-up growing to do. I certainly did, which probably delayed a lot of things and led to a lot of late blooming. But don't despair. Think of going through life as what the character Kandi said on an episode of "Two and a Half Men" about being with Alan: "[It's like being] in the back seat of a car driven by a really smart kangaroo. He may go up on the curb a couple of times, but he'll get you there." The key then is to learn from your faulty high-school days—understand what went wrong, what you did wrong, and learn from it. Adapt accordingly.

Fully Process Rather Than Suppress Your Bad High-School Memories

Now, throwing stuff out doesn't mean simply suppressing your bad high-school memories and feelings. That can be like hiding a ferret in your pants. It could end up eating at your rather sensitive spots over time and emerging at the most unexpected, inopportune times. Instead, consider directly confronting your past and processing it.

In the process, you may even find that your memories don't match reality. The supposedly cool things you missed out on may not have been so cool. Those who made you feel bad may have actually felt very bad about themselves.

In lieu of going to my high-school reunion, I had dinner with someone I actually liked from high school. We had never really talked about our high-school experiences until then. But it soon became apparent that her high-school experience was similarly negative. When you are open about such experiences, you may end up realizing that you weren't quite as alone as you thought you were.

item.title: Should We Ban Brain-Boosting Tech to Protect the Poor?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Should We Ban Brain-Boosting Tech to Protect the Poor?

A ban of human enhancement would not stop the rich. It would hand it to black markets.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • There is no empirical evidence that human enhancement will lead to inequality.
  • Even if human enhancement leads to inequality, it is not clear whether this will outweigh potential benefits.
  • Prohibition is not necessarily the best policy for maximizing well-being.

Recognizing the variety of dystopian science-fiction novels and movies, from Brave New World to Gattaca and, more recently, Star Trek, on the future of humanity in which eugenic policies are implemented, genetic engineering has been getting a bad reputation for valid but, arguably, mostly historical reasons. The same objections are used against technological enhancement of our brains (e.g., computer chips or via drugs). This is why I've published an academic article on the topic.

In this post, I critically examine the claim from Maxwell J. Mehlman and Jeffrey R. Botkin that human enhancement will inevitably accentuate existing inequality in a free market and analyze whether prohibition is the optimal public policy for this objection, as egalitarians might advise. Of course, various moral theories will evaluate this claim, which I shall call the inequality-objection, differently. Yet, for the purposes of the present post, I shall only consider whether the inequality-objection is a problem to the dominant moral framework in policy-making (i.e., utilitarianism).

What Is at Stake?

Though perhaps having raised the largest concerns in the public perception of human enhancement, the inequality-objection is neither a very sophisticated argument nor a very new one, against the introduction of new technologies that could enhance humans beyond what might be considered "normal." In fact, the whole argument is old wine in new bottles. Concerning inequality, Bostrom and Roache claim that one could hold the justified worry that:

People with radically enhanced cognitive capacities might gain vast advantages in terms of income, strategic planning, and the ability to influence others; in other words, an enhanced cognitive elite may gain socially significant amounts of power.

Of course, it seems undesirable if an enhanced elite accumulates a lot of power, but whether this is even a plausible scenario is an open question. From a utilitarian perspective, the inequality-objection can be fleshed out as follows:

  • P1: Human enhancement leads to inequality.
  • P2: Inequality leads to a decrease in well-being.
  • P3: What leads to a decrease in well-being should be prohibited by policy-makers.
  • C: Therefore, human enhancement should be prohibited by policy-makers.

Human Enhancement Leads to Inequality?

Let me begin with the premise that human enhancement will increase inequality. This premise is empirical in nature and, as such, requires supporting evidence. More specifically, there are reasons to believe that human enhancement will not affect inequality at all, or even decrease it, as Bostrom and Roache suggest, by making people “more equal,” as is the case with modafinil. Bostrom suggests that we know far more about genes responsible for inheritable diseases than genes responsible for talents, intelligence, and longevity; hence, human enhancement might especially help the genetically worst-off in society.

article continues after advertisement

This means that some enhancements, like an increase in cognitive capacities, might enable agents to become better competitors. Considering this, it seems unlikely that people wouldn't consider taking loans for enhancing themselves, in order to increase their expected wage. Banks might even give loans for human enhancement in a similar fashion to education loans. Instead of paying for advanced training courses, employers might consider paying for cognitive enhancements of their employees.

Inequality Leads to a Decrease in Well-being?

According to egalitarians, everyone should be equal. Utilitarians, of course, are not concerned with these kinds of egalitarian theories, but rather the maximization of well-being. Several reasons could come to mind: potential oppression, discrimination, unfairness, exploitation, envy, or simply a preference for equality. Even if we grant that these are worrisome consequences of human enhancement, in the utilitarian framework, we would still have to weigh the benefits against these costs. While we may grant that human enhancement might decrease well-being by introducing inequality, there are other areas where human enhancement can potentially increase well-being enormously.

Prohibition of Human Enhancement, the Best Solution?

I argue that it is wrong to think that we have the choice between status quo and a world where human enhancement takes place. Applied to human enhancement, this means that a world where it is illegal does not equal a world where this technology is not available. Anders Sandberg and Nick Bostrom claim that a prohibition will be an incentive for the creation of black markets, which, as with drugs, may tend to make these technologies even more expensive, while legal enhancements would become less risky and less expensive as time goes on. Mehlman and Botkin raise the question of how those breaking the law should be punished—for instance, will someone with genetic enhancements be forced to alter his DNA back to the point it was before or have to be sterilized? Will people who would have died without enhancements have to be sentenced to death by revoking their enhancements?

article continues after advertisement

In short, there are several reasons speaking against prohibition and some that speak in favour of other solutions. For instance, Bostrom proposes subsidies or free access for children of poor families.

Conclusion

There seem to be at least three major problems with the inequality-objection. First, there is no empirical evidence that human enhancement will lead to inequality. Second, even if we accept that human enhancement will lead to inequality, it is not clear whether this will outweigh the potential benefits of human enhancement. Third, even if it does, prohibition is not necessarily the best policy for maximizing well-being. In light of these concerns, I conclude that even if human enhancement leads to inequality, this is not sufficient to conclude that human enhancement should be prohibited by policy-makers.

item.title: Why Do Therapists’ Marriages Fall Apart?
item.description:
Marriage

Why Do Therapists’ Marriages Fall Apart?

The challenges of being married to a therapist.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists help people reflect on their lives and their relationships and turn their problems into solutions.
  • A therapeutic relationship is very different from a personal one.
  • For many therapists, the motivation to enter the profession lies in their own problematic family story.

It would seem intuitive that therapists, having spent many years learning about relationships and how the psyche works, should have strong marriages. They would serve as a personal example and pass on to patients a solidified experience of building robust relationships, bolstered by professional training. However, landmark research by McCoy and Aamodt (2010) showed that among 449 occupations, therapists reported being divorced or separated at a rate higher than the 16.96 percent average (therapists 24.20 percent, social workers 23.16 percent, counselors 22.49 percent).

As I was strolling in the evening, thinking about some personal conundrum, I suddenly came to the realization that I tend to turn every crisis into a lesson. I'm not alone; this is how the therapeutic mind works. Therapists tend to be highly inquisitive; they often love reading; some, like myself, write; and they like to reflect on whatever happens.

This is what drives them in the profession as well. They love helping people reflect on their lives and their relationships and turn their problems into solutions, learning along the way.

However, a therapeutic relationship is very different from a personal one. You could be a therapist married to a spouse who doesn’t see a series of crises as an ongoing invitation to analyze them and extract the lessons.

So what are the difficulties in a therapist’s marriage that could lead to divorce?

Different approaches to handling problems

Therapists are taught to tackle problems head-on, behaviorally or emotionally, depending on the approach. Therapists are usually comfortable engaging in an uncomfortable dialogue about situations, stimulating feelings, often unpleasant ones, or working with deep bodily responses. While all that can serve as great therapeutic tools, in a marriage, the partner might oppose all of them.

The spouse could belong to a large category of people who don't want to deal with problems head-on at all or through processing their emotional response to them, and they postpone dealing with problems until it's impossible not to.

Some therapist-spouses see it as avoidance. They interpret their partners' response as repression or denial, which are considered psychological defenses, so they often attempt to draw out their partner's response whilst the partner is not yet ready to talk about it, or firmly acknowledge the problem. The partner reads this professional bias as impatience and intrusion on boundaries, and its presence multiplies conflicts in a couple.

Compassion fatigue

The therapist's work consists of being empathetic and compassionate, and of caring about other people's feelings. Their spouses believe that this compassion will extend to family members as well. However, having worked with compassion as a sharp tool—often the main tool—therapists find that it tends to get blunt by the evening, by the weekend, or by the end of the year.

Therefore, many therapists can be withdrawn or emotionally exhausted once they get home to their family. They want to be cared for, or they want to be left alone. However, their spouses, and rightfully so, ask for and need their attention and emotional care as well.

It creates the emotional imbalance that many therapists can help their clients deal with quite successfully, yet lack the energy to handle within their own families.

Compassion fatigue goes beyond simply being tired from work. Figley (1995) described it as secondary traumatic stress stemming from having to care for people with trauma and anguish. Common symptoms of compassion fatigue also include sleep difficulties, irritability, general emotional exhaustion, emotional withdrawal, and difficulty in creating genuine empathetic relationships.(3) That's why being in therapy as a therapist can be immeasurably important for work-family balance.

Overthinking relationships

Yes, therapists, especially marriage therapists, learn how to handle relationships, why relationships fail, and how they can be helped. But this very thing causes them to fall into several traps.

Therapists could talk about relationships a lot, and the psychology of relationships as well (the name of my blog, duh), which irritates their partner to no end.

While the subject of relationships might interest therapists a lot, they tend to analyze their own relationship as well, along with their partner's behavior patterns.

What looks like curiosity and a willingness to engage in conversation to the therapist often looks like nit-picking to their partners. The partner often regards the "relationship analysis" as criticism and patronizing.

And here comes another trap, as the therapists' partners often want the opposite of what therapists usually provide to clients. While therapists give their patients containment, holding, therapeutic neutrality, and assistance in creating the environment for the client to grow and change, without the therapist being directly involved in the client's life, the spouses want concrete involvement, actions, and proactive solutions.

Commitment to fixing

For many therapists, the motivation to enter the profession lies in their own problematic family story, such as emotional abuse, parental narcissism, dependencies or addictions among family members, or generational traumas. As research shows (see Deacon et al.), marriage therapists especially crave rewriting the family history, often being the first in generations to disrupt destructive patterns.

However, the therapists' spouses are often not at all motivated or driven by the constant urge to change internally or fix their family story and current relationship. They might want to keep things as they are, appreciating the long-term stability, or they might not want to deal with past traumas at all. So, the drive to change that defines many therapists can be draining for them.

This drive might also make the therapist forget about the role of the partner, and unknowingly assume the role of the therapist within their relationship, putting their spouse and other family members in the role of the client.

Helping with relationships of other people and maintaining one's own long-term relationship differ. That is not to say that the therapist-partner is to be blamed for anything that goes wrong in the relationship—it always takes two to tango—but rather to understand the peculiarities of being a therapist in a marriage or being married to a therapist.

Individual therapy is recommended for the therapist, or for both partners if they deal a lot with people and their emotions outside their relationship. Couples therapy will also be helpful in building supportive communication patterns and restoring the roles of spouses instead of therapist-patient dynamics.

item.title: Tech Outage Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

Tech Outage Anxiety

How to cope when the tech goes down.

Posted November 19, 2026

Key points
  • Even very temporary technological outages can be anxiety-provoking.
  • Hyperreliance on technology has created fears around losing access.
  • Three cognitive distortions can amplify outage anxiety.
  • Humans are grappling with new forms of anxiety related to the recent surge of AI technology.
The November 13 FAA nationwide ground stop was caused by a router/equipment issue during a network upgrade.
Source: Soly Moses / Pexels

This week, millions of Americans experienced the direct effects of a series of major technological outages. Banking, flights, email, the app store, and parts of the government were all disrupted.

While most people were annoyed, some experienced these outages as existential threats. The outages did not feel temporary or safe. Even after the platforms were back up and running, some people were left with a sense of dread.

When we have a hyper-reliance on technology, temporary shutdowns of platforms can makes us feel vulnerable.

The series of outage events this week may have been coincidences, but the anxious brain is unlikely to interpret them as such.

Strong reactions to the outages were most likely amplified by these three common cognitive biases.

  • Overgeneralization. The anxious brain likes to link unrelated events into a general trend. Even if there is no pattern, our anxiety will see a negative pattern and make a generalization.
  • Catastrophization. The anxious brain is more likely to jump to the worst possible outcome. A temporary, safe outage can feel like a permanent danger.
  • Discounting the Positive. Even though most technology worked as usual this week, an anxious brain discounts these positives. This distortion makes us fixate on the problems rather than see them as part of a bigger picture.
Digital Technology is now a permanent fixture in our lives, and in with our anxiety.
Source: Miguel Á. Padriñán / Pexels

On a broader level, people had already been experiencing other forms of technology anxiety.

People with anxiety are hypervigilant to danger, perceived or real. Technology and the ways it could harm us can represent a scary new battleground.

We were also poised to find these outages troubling and stressful because we are already trying to integrate the enormous technological advances of the past few years with artificial intelligence. People are unsettled by the uncertainty of how this technology will change our lives and our livelihoods.

Every new technological advancement brings with it fear about the unknown, but AI perhaps more so than most.

For most laypeople, this advancement has an unsettling sci-fi feel. Many of us feel helpless in the face of the technology’s shocking, exponential growth.

Mental health clinicians must learn to recognize these new subtypes of technology-related anxiety. As a society, we must help each other cope with rapid change, temporary loss of access to technology, and any real danger therein.
